posts.excerpt: A step-by-step guide for community authors who are new to Git and GitHub: fork the blog repository, set up an SSH key, add your post, and open a pull request.
posts.html:
This is an example post for community authors, and it is also the guide. If you have written a post for percona.com/blog but have never opened a pull request, start here. It assumes no Git experience.

If you are a Perconian, you do not need any of the fork steps. You work right in the repository. Read the example post for Perconians instead.

How it works

The blog lives in a GitHub repository. You cannot change it directly, and that is normal for open source: nobody outside the team can. Instead, you make your own copy of the repository, add your post there, and ask us to take it in. Your copy is called a fork, and the request is a pull request.

  1. Fork the blog repository on GitHub. This makes your own copy under your account.
  2. Set up an SSH key, so your computer can send changes to GitHub.
  3. Clone your fork, which downloads it to your computer.
  4. Create a branch for your post.
  5. Add your post and your author page.
  6. Commit the files and push them to your fork.
  7. Open a pull request from your fork to the blog repository.
  8. Reviewers read the post. You push fixes to the same branch.
  9. After three approvals the post is merged and published on percona.com.

The same steps as a diagram:

flowchart TD
  A[Fork the blog repository on GitHub] --> B[Clone your fork to your computer]
  B --> C[Create a branch for your post]
  C --> D[Add the post and your author page]
  D --> E[Commit and push to your fork]
  E --> F[Open a pull request to the blog repository]
  F --> G[Reviewers leave comments]
  G --> H[You push fixes to the same branch]
  H --> G
  G --> I[Three approvals, merged, published on percona.com]

It looks like a lot, but most of it is a one-time setup. Your second post starts at step 4.

What you need

  • A GitHub account. It is free.
  • Git on your computer. On a Mac, run xcode-select --install in the Terminal, or brew install git if you use Homebrew. On Windows, install Git for Windows; it comes with Git Bash, a terminal where every command in this post works.
  • An SSH key. The next sections show how to make one.
  • Your post, in any form: a Google Doc, a Word file, or Markdown.

Let an AI agent help

You do not have to type all of this yourself. AI coding agents such as Cursor and Claude Code are good at exactly this kind of setup: they can install Git, create an SSH key, clone your fork, and turn your draft into a post file. The repository has notes for agents, so they know where files go and which rules to follow.

The easiest start is to give the agent a link to this post or to the blog repository, and your draft:

  • “Here is how to publish a community post on the Percona blog: https://github.com/dbazhenov/percona-test-blog-repo. Help me publish my draft from ~/Downloads/post.docx.”

The agent reads the instructions and walks you through the rest. You can also ask for one step at a time, in plain words:

  • “Help me create an SSH key and add it to my GitHub account.”
  • “Clone my fork of percona-test-blog-repo and create a branch for a new post.”
  • “Turn my draft in ~/Downloads/post.docx into a post for this blog and open a pull request.”

Read what the agent is about to run before you say yes. And never paste your private SSH key into a chat, a form, or an email. Only the public key, the file that ends in .pub, ever goes to GitHub.

Step 1. Fork the repository

Open the blog repository and press Fork in the top right corner. Keep the suggested name and press Create fork.

You now have github.com/<your-username>/percona-test-blog-repo. It is yours: you can push to it, break it, and fix it, and nothing happens to the blog.

Step 2. Set up an SSH key

An SSH key is how GitHub knows that a push really comes from you. It is a pair of files. The private key stays on your computer, and the public key goes to GitHub.

Create the key. Use the email of your GitHub account:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

Press Enter to accept the default file. You can set a passphrase or leave it empty.

Print the public key and copy the whole line:

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

On GitHub, open Settings, then SSH and GPG keys, then New SSH key. Paste the line, give it a name like “My laptop”, and save.

Check that it works:

ssh -T git@github.com

The first time, it asks whether to trust github.com. Type yes. You should see Hi <your-username>! You've successfully authenticated.

If you would rather not deal with SSH, GitHub Desktop signs you in through the browser and does the same steps with buttons. The rest of this post uses the terminal, because that is what an AI agent will use too.

Step 3. Clone your fork

Cloning downloads your fork to your computer. Replace <your-username> with yours:

git clone git@github.com:<your-username>/percona-test-blog-repo.git
cd percona-test-blog-repo

Then tell Git where the original blog repository is. You will need that later to keep your fork up to date:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/dbazhenov/percona-test-blog-repo.git

Step 4. Create a branch

A branch keeps your post separate from everything else. Name it blog/ plus a short name for your post, in lowercase words with hyphens:

git switch -c blog/replication-lag-pt-heartbeat

Step 5. Add your post and your author page

Your post goes into its own folder, posts/<year>/<post-name>/index.md, with its pictures next to it. If this is your first post, you also add an author page, authors/<name-surname>/index.md, with your portrait next to it.

Community posts set origin: community in the front matter, and your author page sets type: community. This post is a first post too, so its pull request adds both: the post in posts/2026/community-post-from-a-fork/ and the author page in authors/mateo-alvarez/, with a square portrait next to it.

The example post for Perconians explains every field, how to choose categories and tags, and which formatting you can use. Everything there applies to you too, except the part about working without a fork. This post is also a working example: look at its folder in the repository.

If you have an AI agent open, this is the step to hand over: give it your draft and ask it to prepare the post.

Step 6. Commit and push

A commit saves your changes in Git. A push sends them to your fork on GitHub:

git add posts authors
git commit -m "Add a post on measuring replication lag"
git push -u origin blog/replication-lag-pt-heartbeat

origin is your fork. You can never push to the blog repository itself, so you cannot break anything by accident.

Step 7. Open the pull request

Open your fork on GitHub. A yellow bar says your branch had recent pushes. Press Compare & pull request.

Check the top of the page: the base should be dbazhenov/percona-test-blog-repo and main, and the head should be your fork and your branch. Give the pull request the title of your post, and fill in the short template: who the post is for, and anything that is missing, such as a cover.

Leave Allow edits by maintainers checked. Then the blog team can fix a typo in your branch without asking you to do it.

Press Create pull request.

Step 8. Review and fixes

Within a few minutes, the first comment on your pull request links to a preview of your post. It shows how the post will look on the blog.

For your first pull request, a maintainer has to approve the automatic checks before they run. That is a GitHub rule for new contributors, and it only happens once.

Reviewers leave comments in the pull request. To fix something, change the file on your computer, then commit and push again to the same branch:

git add posts
git commit -m "Fix the code example"
git push

The pull request and the preview update on their own. You do not need to open a new pull request.

After three approvals, the post is merged and published on percona.com. You do not need to do anything for that.

Your next post

Before you start the next post, bring your fork up to date with the blog:

git switch main
git pull upstream main
git push origin main

Then start again from step 4, with a new branch.

If you get stuck

  • Permission denied (publickey) when you push or clone: GitHub does not know your SSH key. Go back to step 2 and run ssh -T git@github.com.
  • Permission denied or 403 when you push: you are probably pushing to the blog repository instead of your fork. Run git remote -v. origin should point to your username.
  • The checks are red: open the failed check and read the last lines. It names the file and the problem, such as a category that is not on the list or a missing picture.
  • Anything else: ask in the pull request. Reviewers have all been new to this once.

posts.excerpt: How a post gets from your draft to percona.com/blog: the file, the fields, categories and tags, formatting, review, and publishing.
posts.html:
This is an example post, and it is also the instructions. It shows how a Perconian gets a post onto percona.com/blog, and it uses the formatting it describes.

How it works

A post goes from your draft to percona.com in a few steps:

  1. Write the post wherever you like: Google Docs, Word, or straight in Markdown.
  2. Open a pull request in this repository yourself, or ask an AI agent to turn your draft into one.
  3. Open the preview. The first comment on the pull request links to it, so you can see how the post will look on the blog.
  4. Wait for review. Reviewers read the post and leave comments. You answer them and push fixes to the same branch, and the preview updates.
  5. After three approvals, the pull request is merged.
  6. GitHub Actions builds the post and asks percona.com to import it. The post is published.
  7. The publication date is written into your post file, so the repository and the site agree.

The same process as a diagram:

flowchart TD
  A[Write the post in any editor, or in Markdown] --> B[Open a pull request yourself, or ask an AI agent]
  B --> C[The first comment links to the preview]
  C --> D[Reviewers read the post and leave comments]
  D --> E[You push fixes to the same branch]
  E --> D
  D --> F[Three approvals, and the pull request is merged]
  F --> G[GitHub Actions builds the post and asks percona.com to import it]
  G --> H[The post is published on percona.com]
  H --> I[The publication date is written into your post]

You can draw diagrams like this in your own posts. They are written in Mermaid syntax: flowcharts, sequence diagrams, timelines, and more. The source of this one is in “Formatting examples” at the end of this post.

The rest of this post goes through each step.

What a post file looks like

A post file has two parts. At the top, between two --- lines, is the front matter: a few fields about the post, such as the title, the author, and the category. Below it is the text of the post.

A small post looks like this:

---
title: "Why the replica fell behind"
id: why-the-replica-fell-behind
authors:
  - daniil-bazhenov
categories:
  - MySQL
tags:
  - replication
---

Last week a replica on one of our test clusters fell an hour behind.

## What we checked first

The first thing we looked at was the IO thread.

The title from the front matter is shown at the top of the page as the post heading. The text starts right after the closing ---.

Where to put the files

Perconians work right in this repository, without a fork. The Perconians group is added to the repository, so you can create a branch here and push to it. If you cannot push yet, ask the blog team to add you. Community authors do not have that access and work from a fork. The community example post walks through it step by step.

Create a branch from main and name it after the post: blog/ plus the post’s id. This post lives on blog/how-a-perconian-publishes. A fix to a published post goes on fix/ plus the id, for example fix/how-a-perconian-publishes. Use lowercase words with hyphens, without dates or your name. Then anyone looking at the list of branches can tell which post each one is about.

The easiest start is a recent post in posts/: copy its folder, rename it, and replace the text, the pictures, and the fields with your own. Give it a new id and slug, or it will clash with the post you copied. Real posts show how everything fits together better than any template.

A post with pictures is a folder: posts/<year>/<name>/index.md, with the image files next to index.md. In the text you link a picture by its filename, as this post does with steps.png. A post with no pictures can be one file, posts/<year>/<name>.md. Do not put a date in the name.

If this is your first post, add an author page too: authors/<your-id>/index.md, with a square portrait next to it. Your id is name-surname, lowercase, with hyphens. A Perconian sets type: staff. Look at the other folders in authors/ for the fields.

Front matter fields

Field Required What to put there
title Yes The post title. It is the heading at the top of the page.
id Yes A permanent name, the same as the file or folder name. Set it once and do not change it.
slug No Only if the address should differ from id. The address is /blog/<slug>/.
date Yes Any date for the preview. Publishing replaces it with the real publication time.
draft Yes false to publish. true keeps the post off the site and off the feed.
origin Yes percona for a Perconian, community for anyone else.
description No One or two sentences for the post card. Empty means the first paragraph is used.
authors Yes Author ids from authors/, not display names.
categories Yes One to three names from the category list in the next section.
tags No A few words that help readers find related posts. See the next section.
images Yes Files next to the post. The first one is the cover, 1200×630.

The front matter of this post:

title: "Example post: how a Perconian publishes a post"
id: how-a-perconian-publishes
date: "2026-11-12T12:00:00-08:00"
draft: false
origin: percona
description: "How a post gets from your draft to percona.com/blog."
authors:
  - daniil-bazhenov
categories:
  - PostgreSQL
tags:
  - example
images:
  - cover.png
slug: how-a-perconian-publishes

A few things that are easy to get wrong:

  • Changing id after publication makes a second post. Renaming the file is fine as long as id stays the same.
  • The date you type is only for the preview. The real date is set when the post is published, and later edits do not move it.
  • To take a published post down, set draft: true and keep the file. Deleting the file leaves the post on the site.

Categories and tags

Categories are the sections of the blog: readers open percona.com/blog/category/mysql/ and see every MySQL post. A tag is narrower. It says what the post is about inside that section: a tool, a feature, a kind of problem.

Choosing a category

These are the categories that exist on percona.com/blog. Copy the name exactly as it is written here.

Group Categories
Databases MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Valkey
Percona products Percona Server for MySQL, XtraDB Cluster (PXC), Xtrabackup, Percona Monitoring and Management, ProxySQL, Percona Software, Percona Services
Topics Kubernetes, Operator, Cloud, Security, Monitoring, Benchmarks, AI & Vector, Storage Engine, Open Source, Insight for DBAs, Insight for Developers, Database Trends
  • Start with the database. Almost every post has one, and it is the section most readers browse.
  • Add a product if the post is about a Percona product, for example Percona Server for MySQL or Percona Monitoring and Management.
  • Add a topic only if the whole post is about it: a benchmark goes to Benchmarks, a post on running the database in Kubernetes goes to Kubernetes.
  • One to three categories is enough. A post filed everywhere is hard to find anywhere.
  • If the post compares two databases, list both.
  • If nothing fits, do not invent a name. The import does not create categories, so the post would land without one. Ask in the pull request, and the category can be added to the site first.

The front matter of a post about upgrading PostgreSQL with the Percona Operator:

categories:
  - PostgreSQL
  - Kubernetes
  - Operator

Choosing tags

Tags are free text, and the import creates any tag that does not exist yet. That is useful, and it is also how a blog ends up with Benchmarking, Benchmarks, and benchmark as three separate tags. This repository already has that one, and OpenSource next to Opensource.

  • Use two to five tags. More than that stops helping.
  • Before you add a tag, look at what other posts already use, and reuse the same spelling.
  • Name the tool or feature: pgvector, Percona Operator for PostgreSQL, InnoDB, replication.
  • Do not repeat the category as a tag. A PostgreSQL post does not need a PostgreSQL tag.
  • Do not tag your own name, the company, or words like database that fit every post.

Before you ask for review

Look at the post the way readers will see it before you ask anyone to read it. There are two ways to do that, and you only need one.

The preview link in the pull request

This is the easy way, and it needs nothing on your computer. Open the pull request, and within a few minutes the first comment links to a preview of your post. It looks like this:

Every time you push a change to the same branch, the preview is rebuilt.

The pull request also checks the files. If something is wrong, such as a missing author page, a category that is not on the list, or a picture the text names but that is not next to the post, the Feed check turns red and says what to fix.

A preview on your computer

If you want to see the post before you open a pull request, build it locally. You need Hugo 0.168 or newer. From the repository folder, run:

make -C tools serve

Open http://localhost:1314/ . Drafts show up there too, and the page reloads when you save the file.

When the post looks right, stop the preview with Ctrl+C and run the same check the pull request runs:

make -C tools check

It catches the same problems as the Feed check. It does not read the writing.

What happens on the pull request

If you know two or three people who know the subject, ask them to review the pull request. If you do not, just wait: the blog team watches new pull requests and will find reviewers. It is merged after three approvals. If nobody picks it up, or a reviewer declines it, close it and try another post.

While the pull request is open, you edit the post the same way you wrote it. Change the file, commit, and push to the same branch. The preview is rebuilt, and reviewers see the new version in the same pull request. Answer a reviewer’s comment, or resolve it once it is fixed.

Two workflows run on the pull request.

Preview comment posts one comment with a link to your post on the preview site. Each new commit on the same branch rebuilds the preview. The preview shows how the post will look. It is not published. Render deletes it when the pull request is merged or closed.

Feed checks the files while the pull request is open, and publishes when it is merged. Publishing sets the publication date, updates the feed branch, and asks WordPress to import the post. Do not commit to feed yourself. A maintainer can also publish by hand from Actions, Feed, Run workflow. A regular push to main publishes nothing.

Workflow Runs when Does
Preview comment The pull request is opened or updated Comments with a link to the preview
Feed The pull request is opened or updated Checks the files
Feed The pull request is merged Publishes the post
Feed, Run workflow A maintainer starts it Publishes main again

Changing a published post

For the first few days after publication, the post is still yours to fix through the repository. Change the file and open a new pull request, the same way you published it. Say which post it is and what you changed. The publication date stays the same.

After a few days, SEO and content specialists may polish the post. They do not rewrite your text or change what it says. They make small improvements, for example:

  • add or tidy up tags
  • add a call to action at the end
  • adjust headings so search engines and readers understand them better

They make these changes in the WordPress admin panel, not in the repository. If the repository could still update the post, the next import would overwrite their work. So once the post has been polished, editing it through the repository is locked.

You can still ask for a change. Open an issue in this repository, link the post, and describe what should change and why. The team will make the change in WordPress.

Formatting examples

These are the pieces a post can use.

Do not start the text with # Title. Many editors do that, but here the title already comes from title in the front matter. A # heading in the text would be a second title. Start sections at ##. The H2, H3, and H4 headings are shown at the end of this section.

A sentence can use bold, italic, and both. A phrase you took back uses strikethrough. Commands and file names go in inline code, for example make -C tools check.

A link looks like this: Percona Blog.

A quote is for a short remark that should stand apart from the paragraph.

A list:

  • Write the post in Markdown.
  • Put pictures next to index.md.
  • Open a pull request.

A numbered list:

  1. Branch from main.
  2. Add the post.
  3. Open the pull request.

A list inside a list:

  • Before review, check:
    1. The author page exists.
    2. The category is on the list.
    3. Every picture is next to the post.

A checklist:

  • Cover, 1200×630
  • Author page
  • Three approvals

A table:

Piece Where it goes
Post posts/<year>/<name>/index.md
Pictures Next to index.md
Author authors/<id>/index.md

Code, with the language named after the opening fence:

SELECT extname
FROM pg_extension
WHERE extname = 'vector';

A diagram is a Mermaid block. The preview draws it, so you do not need to paste a screenshot. The diagram in “How it works” starts like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Write the post in any editor, or in Markdown] --> B[Open a pull request]
  B --> C[The first comment links to the preview]
```

A picture is an ordinary Markdown image. Put the file next to index.md and use its name:

The text column is 855px wide, so a picture about 1600px wide is enough. Keep each file around 200–400 KB. The cover is 1200×630. An author portrait is a square of about 400px.

H2. A section heading

## starts a section. Every section of this post is an H2.

H3. A subsection heading

### splits a long section.

H4. A smaller heading

#### is the smallest heading you will usually need.

This post is an example, not a product announcement. It shows the Markdown an author can use in a pull request. The first paragraph is the excerpt when description is left empty. Here description is set, so the excerpt comes from that field instead.

Text

A paragraph can use bold, italic, and both. A crossed-out phrase uses strikethrough. File names and commands sit in inline code, for example make -C tools check.

A link can point at a page on the site, such as the Percona Blog, or at a project, such as pgvector.

A block quote is for a short remark you want to set apart from the paragraph above it.

Lists

Unordered:

  • Write the post in Markdown.
  • Put images next to index.md.
  • Open a pull request.

Ordered:

  1. Open the preview.
  2. Read the post.
  3. Approve it or ask for a change.

Nested:

  • Review checks three things:
    1. The author page exists.
    2. The category is one of the known names.
    3. Every image file sits next to the post.

Tasks:

  • Cover, 1200×630
  • Diagram
  • A second review

A figure

The cover is the first name in images. It is the picture at the top of the post. Other pictures are ordinary Markdown images and stay in the article.

Table

Piece Where it goes
Post posts/<year>/slug/index.md
Images Next to index.md
Author authors/<id>/index.md

Code

A fenced block keeps the language name. This one is SQL:

SELECT extname
FROM pg_extension
WHERE extname = 'vector';

Diagram

A diagram is a Mermaid block. The preview draws it, so a screenshot is not required.

flowchart LR
  Write --> Review --> Published

A shorter heading

Detail

A note under the detail

posts.excerpt: Type “zero downtime database migration” into the site’s search bar and you’ll get articles and talks about database migration with minimal downtime, even if those words aren’t in the titles or content. This is semantic search on PostgreSQL and pgvector, without paid embedding APIs or a separate vector database. In this series I’ll cover how it works and why I chose this stack. I’ll walk through how and why I built the search for our community site: blog, events, talks, and profiles. The post should help if you want to repeat the approach or need a practical case study on simple components. If you’ve done something similar, I’d like to hear your feedback.
posts.html:
Type “zero downtime database migration” into the site’s search bar and you’ll get articles and talks about database migration with minimal downtime, even if those words aren’t in the titles or content. This is semantic search on PostgreSQL and pgvector, without paid embedding APIs or a separate vector database. In this series I’ll cover how it works and why I chose this stack.

I’ll walk through how and why I built the search for our community site: blog, events, talks, and profiles. The post should help if you want to repeat the approach or need a practical case study on simple components. If you’ve done something similar, I’d like to hear your feedback.

Context: Website, Search, and Task

The community team has a website on Hugo, an open source static site generator, hosted for free on GitHub Pages. The site has articles, events, talks, videos, and more.

If you’re thinking of starting your own, I recommend checking out these examples: blog.koehntopp.info, openeverest.io, perconalive.com, oursqlfoundation.org

But a Hugo site is a collection of HTML files without a backend. Search or filters only work via frontend JS or an external service. For a long time our site had no search at all. Then Kai Wagner contributed a JS search for the blog that matched exact words (percona.community/blog).

Recently our community lead Laura Czajkowski asked for smart AI search on the site. We tried several off-the-shelf products; they were either too expensive or a poor fit. We also want search to cover more than the site itself eventually: videos from other platforms, the forum, our GitHub repos, and maybe documentation later.

I suggested building it ourselves. Modern AI assistants are good enough for a prototype like this. Below I’ll explain the stack.

What We’ll Do

The site stays on Hugo and GitHub Pages. The search service runs separately; for this architecture that’s the sensible option. The goal is simple: the user types a query in plain language and gets a list of semantically relevant links.

Kai’s keyword search was a step forward, but it doesn’t catch meaning. Type “postgresql” and you get pages where the word appears. An article about slow queries or replication may be missing if the wording is different. Semantic search works differently: the query and documents become vectors, numeric representations of meaning (embedding). Similar meaning lands nearby in vector space even when the words differ. A query like “how to speed up slow queries in MySQL” can surface tuning and optimization content without those words in the title.

Why not another engine? OpenSearch is a solid open-source option: full-text and vector search, mature ecosystem. I also looked at Manticore Search. Both work, but semantics still need an embedding pipeline (model at index time and on each query). That’s another service to run beside the model.

I wanted my own stack on Postgres with pgvector: a practical experiment, not a hunt for the perfect search product. PostgreSQL with pgvector keeps page metadata, chunks, vectors, and query history in one database. Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL 18 ships pgvector in the distribution; run CREATE EXTENSION vector and you’re set.

The plan has four parts:

  1. Widget on the site: search field and results (plain JS; Hugo unchanged).
  2. API: takes the query, embeds it with the same model as indexing, searches the DB, returns JSON links.
  3. Indexer: background worker that reads RSS/HTML, chunks text, embeds, writes to the DB.
  4. PostgreSQL + pgvector: one database for metadata, chunks, vectors, and search history.

Hugo stays static; the smart parts live in a separate service. No separate vector DB, no paid embedding API, no RAG chat, only links.

The diagram shows two flows: search (user query) and indexing (refresh the DB on demand or on a schedule). Top to bottom, from the user:

flowchart TB
    User(["👤 User"])

    Widget["🔍 JS widget<br/>percona.community · GitHub Pages"]

    API["⚡ FastAPI<br/>search.percona.community"]

    Model["🧠 Embedding model<br/>shared · API & indexer"]

    DB[("🗄️ PostgreSQL + pgvector")]

    Content["📰 Content<br/>blog · events · talks"]

    Indexer["📥 Indexer worker"]

    User -->|"① query"| Widget
    Widget -->|"② POST /search"| API
    API <-->|embed query| Model
    API <-->|"③ vector search"| DB
    API -->|"④ results"| Widget
    Widget --> User

    Content -->|"A. RSS + HTML"| Indexer
    Indexer <-->|embed chunks| Model
    Indexer -->|"B. chunks + vectors"| DB

    style User fill:#e1f5ff
    style Widget fill:#fff4e6
    style Content fill:#fff9e6
    style API fill:#ffe6e6
    style Model fill:#fff0f5
    style Indexer fill:#f0e6ff
    style DB fill:#e6ffe6

The diagram shows the shared embedding model; worth stating explicitly anyway. The indexer and the API must use the same model. Query vectors and stored vectors must share one space or search is meaningless. Don’t mix Nomic at index time with OpenAI at query time, for example. The widget only sends text; it doesn’t know which model runs behind the API.

On paper it looked simple. In practice I changed the database schema three times and tuned ranking so blog posts didn’t crowd out events and talks. The similarity threshold mattered more than I expected: one parameter, large swing in results. Still, within a few days we had a working beta on the live site. Here’s what shipped.

The Result (Spoiler)

It took about three unhurried days and roughly $20 in Cursor tokens to build, debug, and deploy. Try it on percona.community (search icon in the header) or percona.community/search/.

The index currently covers the site: blog, events, talks, member profiles. Video from other platforms, the forum, and GitHub are planned; the design should allow new sources without replacing the stack.

This is beta: the content is public and search isn’t business-critical, but I watch stability and security.

Website Widget

The header has a search icon. Click it to get an input field and a popup with results, similarity score (0 to 1, how close the hit is in meaning), and API latency. The site stays static; the widget calls search.percona.community and renders JSON. “All results” opens /search/.

Try it on percona.community, e.g. slow queries mysql tuning or kubernetes operator database. Comments welcome if something feels off.

Full Results Page

A separate /search/ page with filters by content type, cards, and links.

Example

API

FastAPI at https://search.percona.community: embed the query, search Postgres, return JSON with links, scores, and timings (model vs database).

The service runs on AWS EC2 in Docker Compose: API, indexer, Postgres.

Demo Dashboard

The Cursor AI agent handled a lot of the boilerplate, so I also built a dev dashboard (/demo) to test search, run indexing, inspect history, and browse indexed chunks. Not for production, but it saved debugging time.

Demo Dashboard

Search history: making search better

Indexing status, to see when search data was last updated

Indexed documents with the ability to view data and chunks.

What I Used

Briefly, why this stack (deeper comparison in part two):

  • PostgreSQL + pgvector: vectors and metadata in one DB. Cosine similarity plus an HNSW index is enough at community scale. (pgvector in Percona docs)

  • Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL 18: PostgreSQL with pgvector and a Docker image. Vanilla Postgres works too if you install the extension; I used Percona to try “their” Postgres + pgvector in a real deploy.

  • Python + FastAPI: fast API setup, OpenAPI included, good libraries for crawl/embed/Postgres.

  • nomic-embed-text-v1 + sentence-transformers: open model, 768 dims, CPU-friendly, no per-chunk API bill. Index and query must use the same model; Nomic fits. I’ll compare others later.

  • Hugo + JavaScript: thin widget on existing static site.

  • Docker / Docker Compose: same layout locally and on EC2.

  • AWS EC2 + nginx: HTTPS on search.percona.community, CORS for GitHub Pages.

  • AI-assisted development (I used Cursor): the agent handled boilerplate, wiring, and Docker fixes. I reviewed everything. Any similar AI coding tool would work; the point is having one.

How long it took

  • ~6 hours with an AI coding assistant to a first prototype: crawl, API, Docker, basic demo;
  • ~2 more days for schema changes, per-type ranking, embed/page widget, search history, dashboard, indexer fixes, EC2 deploy;
  • ~$20 in AI assistant tokens total.

Without AI I’d have stretched the same work over weeks. With the agent I mostly wrote tasks, checked output, and fixed edges.

About the code and repository

I’m not publishing the repo yet. The code is tied to percona.community: our RSS feeds, content types, Hugo widget, EC2 layout. It’s an internal prototype, not a reusable library.

If you wanted a drop-in repo: porting someone else’s monolith often takes longer than rebuilding from a clear sketch. Part two will have architecture, schema, and stack notes enough for a Cursor agent (or similar) to rebuild for your feeds and UI.

Interested in a generic open source or search-as-a-service version? Say so in the comments; I’m weighing whether it’s worth a separate project.

What’s Next

Try search on percona.community and comment what you find, especially where semantics beat the old substring search.

Part two will go inside: schema (including those three rewrites), chunking, HNSW, per-type result caps, and a local Docker Compose walkthrough.

posts.html:
It was quite challenging to perform postgres major upgrade, e.g., v17 to v18, in a Percona operator/K8s environment. There was no convenient approach to accomplish this task. The only viable solutions left were a Manual Dump/Restore to a new environment or using Logical replication.

But these options were not free from challenges. Procuring a new Infrastructure/Cluster or running the manual process is complex and error-prone. Logical replication has its own caveats; not everything can be replicated smoothly using the native logical option.

Moreover, performing a manual pg_upgrade (In-Place) in the Operator/K8S environment is risky and unsupported.

This problem was addressed effectively by our engineering team, and they released a technical release of the Major Upgrade option under Postgres Operator v2.4.0. After a couple of releases, the Major Upgrade feature finally became generally available (GA) under operator v2.9.0.

  • Under the hood, the major upgrade activity in the operator runs InPlace(pg_upgrade) triggered by the PerconaPGUpgrade resource.
  • The Operator then pauses the cluster and shuts it down.
  • The upgrade Job runs “pg_upgrade –link” on the primary’s volume, creating the new data directory (pg17) alongside the old one (pg16).
  • Replicas are then re-synced from the upgraded primary.
  • Finally, the cluster restarts on the new version.

Minimum Requirements and Considerations

  • Percona Operator for PostgreSQL v2.4.0 (Tech Release); however, it’s better to upgrade to v2.9.0, which is officially GA.
  • If the OS version and the glibc library change after the upgrade, they need to be addressed or fixed.
  • The extensions need to be cross-validated, whether or not they are upgraded. Some extensions, such as the pgaudit extension, are not automatically upgraded. That needs to be dropped and recreated in each database where it is installed.
  • The major upgrade activity invalidates (removes) any existing logical replicas that are already in place. After the upgrade, verify and reseed the logical replicas.

If you are still running a pretty old Operator version, it must be upgraded to at least the latest Operator v2.4.0-1 https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.0.0/update-operator.html to avail the “Major Upgrade” feature.

Let’s see, step by step and in detail, how we can accomplish the major upgrade.

Existing Operator/DB Environment:

Operator Version: v2.4.0

  • Since operator v2.6.0, the base OS image has changed from ubi8 to ubi9: https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPG-652 & https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.1.0/ReleaseNotes/Kubernetes-Operator-for-PostgreSQL-RN2.6.0.html#improvements, which will result in a change in the glibc version from v2.28 to v2.34. Considering this, we have to address the impact of the collation change after the upgrade: https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.0.0/update-db-major.html#check-collation.
  • The custom-built images (https://github.com/percona/percona-docker/blob/main/postgresql-containers/README.md) could be an option for using the existing UBI8 images with v2.6.0 (pg17); however, that is not a recommended path and may lead to errors or failures unless thoroughly tested. Production Readiness(Before you upgrade):

Although most upgrades are expected to deliver improvements, even a small number of edge cases can introduce regressions with significant business impact, including production outages. New PostgreSQL versions may also introduce behavioural changes or depreciate or remove existing features.

Therefore, for production environments, we strongly recommend at least three trial upgrade rounds, followed by thorough application validation before the final upgrade and cutover.

Conclusion:

The PostgreSQL major upgrade process we discussed above is not limited to upgrading between consecutive major versions. We can also perform in-place upgrades across larger version gaps, such as PostgreSQL 15 to 17, provided the applicable version compatibility requirements are met.

This feature significantly simplifies major version upgrade activities and reduces the associated operational effort. However, particularly when upgrading to Operator version 2.4.0 (where this feature was first introduced as a technical release), or when adopting it for the first time in subsequent versions, it is strongly recommended to thoroughly validate the process in a non-production or staging environment. As discussed earlier, several compatibility considerations and potential post-upgrade fixes need to be evaluated and addressed before allowing application traffic to resume in the upgraded environment.

If the upgrade fails or gets stuck for any reason, it can be resumed using the older PostgreSQL version: https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.0.0/pause.html. Further, the PerconaPGUpgrade resource and cluster/pod-level logs (see https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/3.0.0/update-db-major.html#troubleshooting-upgrade-issues) can be checked to identify the issue.

posts.excerpt: In my previous post I said that MongoDB published some impressive numbers for 9.0, but I couldn’t find any details about how the tests were done. I ended with “always run your own benchmarks”. So I figured I should follow my own advice. Let me be clear up front: this is a first, quick test, not an extensive benchmark by any means. It’s one workload, one hardware configuration for three different data sizes. Treat the numbers as an early indication, not a verdict. I’m sharing them anyway, together with everything you need to do your own tests.
posts.html:
In my previous post I said that MongoDB published some impressive numbers for 9.0, but I couldn’t find any details about how the tests were done. I ended with “always run your own benchmarks”. So I figured I should follow my own advice. Let me be clear up front: this is a first, quick test, not an extensive benchmark by any means. It’s one workload, one hardware configuration for three different data sizes. Treat the numbers as an early indication, not a verdict. I’m sharing them anyway, together with everything you need to do your own tests.

Test setup

Infrastructure

I deployed everything with PSMDB Sandbox on Google Cloud. Each version ran on its own three-node replica set, and the three replica sets were identical except for the MongoDB package version:

Versions tested:

  • mongo9: MongoDB Community 9.0.4
  • psmdb80: Percona Server for MongoDB 8.0.34-15
  • psmdb83: Percona Server for MongoDB 8.3.13-4

Note: PSMDB is built from the same upstream code, and none of the PSMDB-specific features were enabled in order to keep the configuration as similar as possible.

Workload

I used PLGM’s built-in “flights” workload (collection airline.flights, 7 secondary indexes):

  • 60% finds (flight_id $in lookups)
  • 20% updates (updateOne by flight_id, updateMany by _id)
  • 10% deletes (deleteOne by flight_id, deleteMany by _id)
  • 10% inserts (batches of 10 documents)
  • Writes use the server’s default write concern, so they include replication.
  • 16 workers, with no think time: each worker sends its next command as soon as the previous one returns
  • Collections are dropped and seeded again before each iteration.

I ran the workload three times, with three data sizes:

Queries read the seeded documents, while inserts keep adding new ones, so the collection grows during the run. “Fits in RAM” here means the compressed data still fits in the operating system’s file cache, so a WiredTiger cache miss usually doesn’t need a disk read. With 8M documents, the compressed collection is about as big as the server’s entire memory. The compression ratio is about 2:1, so 25% of the documents can fit in WTcache. All runs were deterministic. Each command is generated from a fixed seed, iteration, worker and operation number, so every MongoDB version received exactly the same commands with the same values, and in the same order for each worker. Each worker had a pass of 250,000 commands per iteration. In the 1M and 4M runs every version finished at least one full pass, and PLGM’s traffic fingerprints matched. In the 8M run the servers were too slow to finish a pass in 30 minutes, so each version sent the first 2.7–2.8M commands of the same sequence. PLGM flags that as incomplete. Because the commands are still identical, I compared them operation by operation anyway. PLGM ran the three versions one after another, so each one had the load generator to itself.

Results

At a glance

Figure 1: Throughput with 1M, 4M and 8M documents. Percentages are relative to MongoDB 9.0.4.

Figure 2: Average latency with 1M, 4M and 8M documents.

Figure 3: Throughput over time with 1M documents, in 1-minute averages. Each line is plotted on its own run clock.

Figure 4: Throughput over time with 4M documents, in 1-minute averages. 9.0 stayed ahead for the whole run.

Figure 5: Throughput over time with 8M documents, in 1-minute averages. The three lines overlap most of the time.

Latency percentiles

Figure 6: Average, median, p95 and p99 latency with 4M and 8M documents. With 4M documents 9.0 is ahead on every percentile; with 8M documents the tails are about the same.

Figure 7: How much higher (or lower) the average latency of 8.0 and 8.3 was than 9.0, by query type, for each data size. The pattern changes with the data size. With 1M documents, 9.0’s advantage over 8.0 was mostly in writes. With 4M documents, finds show the biggest difference (+12%). With 8M documents, the single-document updates and deletes by flight_id, which have to fetch a document that is probably not in memory, were the same on all three versions or even slightly faster on 8.0. 9.0 stayed ahead on finds, inserts and the _id-based operations.

Query plans

After each run, PLGM ran explain on samples of each type of query. All three versions chose exactly the same plans with every data size:

  • finds: LIMIT → FETCH → IXSCAN on flight_id_1_equipment.plane_type_1
  • updates and deletes by flight_id: UPDATE/DELETE → FETCH → IXSCAN on the same index
  • updateMany and deleteMany by _id: EXPRESS_UPDATE and EXPRESS_DELETE on id

So the differences are not caused by different plans.

How to repeat the test

You can run the same or a different test yourself, and I’d encourage you to do so.

1. Deploy the environment

With PSMDB Sandbox (web UI or tfvars), create a GCP environment with three replica sets, a PLGM host and PMM:

region                 = "northamerica-northeast1"
zone_mode              = "single"
compact_placement      = true
replsetsvr_type        = "n2-standard-4"
replsetsvr_volume_size = 80
data_disk_type         = "pd-ssd"
min_cpu_platform       = "Intel Ice Lake"
nic_type               = "GVNIC"
enable_pmm             = true
enable_plgm            = true
plgm_type              = "n2-highcpu-8"

clusters = {}
replsets = {
  mongo9 = {
    data_nodes_per_replset = 3
    mongodb_distribution   = "community"
    mongo_release          = "9.0"
    mongo_version          = "9.0.4"
    enable_pbm             = false
    enable_mongot          = false
  }
  psmdb80 = {
    data_nodes_per_replset = 3
    mongodb_distribution   = "psmdb"
    mongo_release          = "psmdb-80"
    mongo_version          = "8.0.34"
  }
  psmdb83 = {
    data_nodes_per_replset = 3
    mongodb_distribution   = "psmdb"
    mongo_release          = "psmdb-83"
    mongo_version          = "8.3.13"
  }
}

PLGM comes pre-installed on the PLGM host. Open an SSH tunnel with ssh -F _ssh_config -plgm, then go to http://127.0.0.1:29999. The connection string for each replica set is displayed on the environment page.

2. Run PLGM

In the web UI, choose Run a generic workload and set Run on to Several servers. Then enter the settings below. If you prefer the command line, here are the settings for the 1M run as environment variables:

export PLGM_DEFAULT_WORKLOAD=true
export PLGM_DOCUMENTS_COUNT=1000000
export PLGM_DROP_COLLECTIONS=true
export PLGM_CONCURRENCY=16
export PLGM_DURATION=30m
export PLGM_ITERATIONS=3
export PLGM_INTERVAL_DELAY=5m
export PLGM_FIND_PERCENT=60
export PLGM_UPDATE_PERCENT=20
export PLGM_DELETE_PERCENT=10
export PLGM_INSERT_PERCENT=5
export PLGM_BULK_INSERT_PERCENT=5
export PLGM_AGGREGATE_PERCENT=0
export PLGM_TRANSACTION_PERCENT=0
export PLGM_INSERT_BATCH_SIZE=10
export PLGM_FIND_BATCH_SIZE=10
export PLGM_FIND_LIMIT=5
export PLGM_READ_PREFERENCE=secondary
export PLGM_RANDOM_SEED=178477
export PLGM_WORKLOAD_DETERMINISTIC=true
export PLGM_OPERATIONS_PER_WORKER=250000
export PLGM_WORKLOAD_RECORD_OUTCOMES=true
export PLGM_WORKLOAD_DETERMINISTIC_OUTCOMES_PATH=/var/lib/plgm/outcomes.ndjson
export PLGM_WORKLOAD_REPLAY_TARGETS_MODE=sequential
export PLGM_WORKLOAD_REPLAY_TARGETS="mongo9=mongodb://:@/?replicaSet=mongo9;psmdb80=mongodb://...;psmdb83=mongodb://..."
plgm

For the 4M run, change PLGM_DOCUMENTS_COUNT=4000000 and PLGM_ITERATIONS=1. For the 8M run, use PLGM_DOCUMENTS_COUNT=8000000 and PLGM_ITERATIONS=1. With the same seed and settings you should get the same traffic fingerprints I got: c0a88fae… for the 1M run and 9734a782… for the 4M run. More useful than this benchmark is to use your own workload. PLGM can run with your own custom collection definitions and queries, or replay traffic captured from your mongod logs.

To sum up

In this quick test, MongoDB 9.0 used less CPU per operation than 8.0 and 8.3 with every data size. That made it about 6% faster when the CPU was the bottleneck, but only about 2% faster when the data fit comfortably in memory or when the disk was the limit. The query plans were the same everywhere. 8.3 was the slowest of the three whenever the CPU mattered. That’s a nice improvement, but on its own it isn’t a reason to upgrade in a hurry. Before you expect anything from 9.0, find out what limits your own servers. Next, I want to repeat the test a few more times, try different levels of concurrency and faster disks, and look at why 8.3 needs more CPU. I’ll share the results in a follow-up post. Like I said in my previous post, treat 9.0 as a release to test, not one you have to deploy urgently. And if you run some tests yourself, I’d like to hear what you get.

posts.excerpt: Unlike row-oriented databases, which store data for a single record sequentially on disk, favoring single-row lookups, columnar databases store all the values from a column contiguously in storage, allowing only the selected column to be read from disk.
posts.html:
MySQL and DuckDB

Unlike row-oriented databases, which store data for a single record sequentially on disk, favoring single-row lookups, columnar databases store all the values from a column contiguously in storage, allowing only the selected column to be read from disk.

The default MySQL engine is InnoDB, which is ACID-compliant and great for OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) workloads. That said, OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) queries are built differently; they scan, group, and summarize millions or billions of rows to produce reports. In these cases, the InnoDB engine can be slow to process such queries. This has been a debt in MySQL over the years; it was common to setup ETL/CDC pipelines to export or stream the data to another engine, usually a columnar database system, to run reporting and BI queries on it.

DuckDB is a portable analytical database system, designed to be fast and reliable, similar to SQLite.

Recently, various vendors (MariaDB, Alibaba) started including DuckDB inside MySQL as a storage engine. A table declared with ENGINE=DuckDB stores data in columnar format, and queries are handled by the DuckDB engine.

This is useful in several ways; the main one is to use MySQL asynchronous replication to stream data from the OLTP, using the InnoDB engine, to a Replica where tables are in DuckDB, thereby offloading the OLAP workload to the replica. To showcase this, we thought that the best example was an on-line store which naturally requires both: short, fast, scalable transactions for the store frontend, and analytics for the store’s reporting and Business Intelligence, and what better than the free and open-source software that serves between 20 and 40% of the world’s e-commerce websites: WooCommerce.

WooCommerce

There are around 4M WooCommerce stores worldwide, the most of any e-commerce platform, handling between 20 and 39% of all e-commerce sites, and they use MySQL as their underlying database.

One of the reasons stores have been adopting computers for over 50 years, is the value of having accumulated information about your business’ transactions. This data collection allows business owners to understand trends and find new opportunities, by turning raw data into metrics that marketing and sales departments can act upon. This process is based on the long-term accumulation of large amounts of data and metadata, and that accumulation is often incompatible with transactional/row-oriented storage engines.

WooCommerce has a built-in analytics module to create those reports that provide metrics, so it is the perfect product to test the performance difference between InnoDB and DuckDB.

WooCommerce analytics does not run its reports against live order tables because querying these tables would be too slow. Instead, it keeps a set of aggregations in a number of denormalized “lookup” tables, which are optimized for this purpose. This is a limitation when running reports with InnoDB, as querying the raw tables would kill performance, and thus the reports are limited to what you can get from these lookup tables.

The following lookup tables are created for WooCommerce Analytics:

mysql> SHOW TABLES LIKE '%wc_%lookup'; SHOW TABLES LIKE '%wc_order_stats';
+-------------------------------------+
| Tables_in_woocommerce (%wc_%lookup) |
+-------------------------------------+
| wp_wc_category_lookup               |
| wp_wc_customer_lookup               |
| wp_wc_order_coupon_lookup           |
| wp_wc_order_product_lookup          |
| wp_wc_order_tax_lookup              |
| wp_wc_product_attributes_lookup     |
| wp_wc_product_meta_lookup           |
+-------------------------------------+
7 rows in set (0.00 sec)

+-----------------------------------------+
| Tables_in_woocommerce (%wc_order_stats) |
+-----------------------------------------+
| wp_wc_order_stats                       |
+-----------------------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

The wp_wc_order_stats table is the spine of the revenue and orders reports; it contains one row per order, including dates, status, customer, number of items sold, and the monetary totals.

In the store we’re using, the wc_order_stats table contains 400000 rows, and there are 5000 products. This data was loaded using the WooCommerce Smooth Generator plugin.

The lookup tables are derived data, so WooCommerce has to keep them in sync with the orders they summarize, which it does in the background (which means you have to run a scheduled process that is what keeps these lookup tables updated).

MySQL Deployment

We deployed a Source/Replica MySQL topology with both databases on the same host, each with its respective Docker image.

Source

The Source runs Percona Server for MySQL 8.0.46, which we chose to match the replica’s major version.

WooCommerce tables use the MySQL default engine, which is InnoDB.

We configured an InnoDB Buffer Pool of 4 GiB:

[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size=4G

Replica

For this test, as a Replica we deployed AliSQL 8.0.44-2, Alibaba’s MySQL branch based on MySQL 8.0.44, which includes the DuckDB storage engine along with other features such as Vector Search and Flashback. At this moment, this is the latest available version.

We configured the DuckDB instance with the following settings:

[mysqld]
duckdb_memory_limit=4G    # maximum memory DuckDB is allowed to use
force_innodb_to_duckdb=ON # force-replace the InnoDB engine with DuckDB
duckdb_threads=0          # total number of threads used by DuckDB. 0 equals system CPU cores.

You can find full reference for DuckDB settings here https://github.com/alibaba/AliSQL/blob/master/wiki/duckdb/duckdb_variables-en.md

The force_innodb_to_duckdb option is mandatory in this process, as it is the way to tell MySQL to use DuckDB engine for tables created via replication or mysqldump.

After loading the 5000 products and 400K orders, the size of the WooCommerce database directory using the InnoDB engine was 7.3 GiB:

$ du -sch woocommerce/
7.3G woocommerce/

While on the replica where tables have been created with DuckDB, the dataset fits in just 601 MiB:

$ du -sch duckdb.db
601M duckdb.db

That is a solid 12x improvement on disk footprint!

Sending reports queries directly to the Replica

We wanted to find a way to make the process as transparent as possible, but WooCommerce uses WordPress’s single database connection object for everything, which means that the reports’ code will use the global $wpdb, and there is no setting that would allow us to send this reporting/analytics traffic to a different server, or an easy way to introduce a second connection object to the code. This means you are stuck with a single server, so there would be no easy way to make use of both InnoDB and DuckDB copies.

Thus, we had to come up with some solution to run the reports against the replica. We like simple stuff, so instead of changing the existing WooCommerce installation at all, we run a whole second copy of the same WooCommerce installation that connects to the replica, and we push the analytics traffic to that second WooCommerce copy.

The original install of your store stays exactly as it is, with its wp-config.php which already points to the primary (InnoDB/transactional) database:

define( 'DB_HOST', 'ps8.example.local' );   // Percona Server for MySQL 8.0.46, InnoDB

And the second install is just a full copy of the first, in its own directory, with just one line of code changed: the database host.

$ cp -aL /var/www/html /var/www/html2;  # we assume your WooCommerce install is /var/www/html 
$ chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html2 # and we also assume you run Apache; should not be hard to adapt for Nginx or other web servers

In the copy’s wp-config.php we change only the host and leave the table prefix, the authentication keys, everything else untouched:

define( 'DB_HOST', 'duckdb8.example.local'' );  // AliSQL 8.0.44 with the DuckDB storage engine, the replica

The second install gets a dedicated pool, listening on its own socket, and its own virtual host on an internal port, handing .php to that pool:

# /etc/httpd/conf.d/html2.conf
<VirtualHost 127.0.0.1:8080>
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html2
    <Directory "/var/www/html2">
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
    <FilesMatch \.php$>
        SetHandler "proxy:unix:/run/php-fpm/www2.sock|fcgi://localhost"
    </FilesMatch>
</VirtualHost>

With that in place, we have two addresses for (essentially) the same WooCommerce, each using a different database:

– http://127.0.0.1:80/ is the store, on Percona Server for MySQL 8.0.46 (InnoDB).

– http://127.0.0.1:8080/ is the copy, on DuckDB replica.

Every analytics call we benchmark goes to one or the other, so the same report is run against InnoDB and against DuckDB from the same codebase, changing nothing but the database underneath.

Benchmark Methodology

Each report was run several times, and we kept the fastest run for each.

Before comparing times, we verified that both engines returned the same result set: the same number of rows and the same values, once serialized and sorted. A few reports differed because the DuckDB engine computes decimals as double-precision floating-point rather than exact DECIMAL, so some monetary sums ended up a fraction of a cent apart. While this might be of concern when dealing with real money, for reporting the precision DuckDB provides should be more than enough, as the difference between the reports was always below 1 cent.

The two engines never ran at the same time. Every report ran first on InnoDB and then on DuckDB, so they never competed for CPU, memory, or disk (at the web server layer).

A few reports whose SQL relied on MySQL-only syntax failed outright on DuckDB and were discarded rather than rewritten, since the point was to run the same query on both engines.

We drove the benchmarks through WooCommerce’s own Analytics REST API, sending the same report requests to each engine and timing the responses.

Each report was run with the force_cache_refresh parameter, so the result is computed from the database on every call rather than served from WooCommerce’s cache.

Built-in Analytics Reports

We started with the built-in WooCommerce Analytics reports. All reports used the same window, from 2024-01-01 to 2026-09-01, over a store of 400,000 orders. The stats reports were aggregated by month; the detail reports returned up to 100 rows per page.

Every built-in report ran faster on DuckDB, from about 10x to nearly 63x, and all of them finished in under a second against InnoDB’s 5 to 16. The biggest improvement resulted from the category reports, where the heavy grouping and aggregation show the columnar engine’s strength.

Built-in Analytics Segmented Reports

The built-in reports are not limited to a single total over a date range. Each stats report takes an interval, so you can ask for the same figures broken down by hour, day, week, or month, and several of them also accept a segmentby parameter, which splits the totals along a dimension. Segmenting by category, for example, returns revenue or order numbers per product category rather than as a single combined figure, which is how the Analytics screens generate their breakdowns.

The finer the interval and the more segments involved, the more the report asks of the database. These are the reports we use to compare InnoDB and DuckDB because they are where the underlying engine makes the most difference.

Every segmented report ran faster on DuckDB, ranging from about 14x to 83x faster. Segmenting by category and time pushes InnoDB into multi-minute queries, while DuckDB still answers in seconds, so the heavier the breakdown, the wider the gap.

WooCommerce Customer Analytics Plugin

To see whether the engine helps with real third-party code, not just the built-in reports, we also benchmarked the Customer Analytics for WooCommerce plugin from Coddium.

It extends WooCommerce Analytics with customer metrics the built-in reports do not provide: customer lifetime value, churn rate, RFM segments, cohort retention, repeat purchase rate, order sequence, and acquisition sources, among others.

Like the built-in reports, each of these reads from the same WooCommerce Analytics lookup tables, making it a good test of whether a plugin written for MySQL runs faster on the DuckDB engine without any changes of its own.

Even with a third-party plugin we did not modify, all eleven reports ran faster on DuckDB, from about 2x to nearly 70x faster.

Ad-hoc Query on Live Data

As mentioned, the built-in analytics reports are served from precomputed lookup tables, which only answer the questions they were designed to answer. For anything else, you have to query the live order tables directly. So we tested an expensive query against those tables to compare the performance.

In this case, we wanted to know how many items were sold, broken down by product category, city, and day of the week, across the store’s orders in the date range. We came up with the following query:

SELECT
  tt.term_taxonomy_id                            AS category_id,
  LOWER(a.city)                                  AS city,
  DAYOFWEEK(o.date_created_gmt)                  AS dow,
  SUM(CAST(im_qty.meta_value AS DECIMAL(10,2)))  AS items_sold
FROM woocommerce.wp_wc_orders o
JOIN woocommerce.wp_wc_order_addresses a
  ON a.order_id = o.id AND a.address_type = 'billing'
JOIN woocommerce.wp_woocommerce_order_items oi
  ON oi.order_id = o.id AND oi.order_item_type = 'line_item'
JOIN woocommerce.wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta im_prod
  ON im_prod.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id AND im_prod.meta_key = '_product_id'
JOIN woocommerce.wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta im_qty
  ON im_qty.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id AND im_qty.meta_key = '_qty'
JOIN woocommerce.wp_term_relationships tr
  ON tr.object_id = CAST(im_prod.meta_value AS DECIMAL(20,0))
JOIN woocommerce.wp_term_taxonomy tt
  ON tt.term_taxonomy_id = tr.term_taxonomy_id AND tt.taxonomy = 'product_cat'
WHERE o.type = 'shop_order'
  AND o.status IN ('wc-completed','wc-processing')
  AND o.date_created_gmt >= '2024-01-01' AND o.date_created_gmt < '2026-09-01'
GROUP BY category_id, LOWER(a.city), dow;

The execution time difference between both engines can be found below:

Across three runs each, DuckDB was consistently about 4.1 seconds and InnoDB about 4 minutes 16 seconds.

The results are not identical, and the two extra groups come from how each engine compares text. Since the city column uses a case- and accent-insensitive collation that InnoDB applies, it folds an accented spelling and its plain form into a single group. The DuckDB engine does not apply the collation and compares text byte-for-byte, keeping them apart.

No orders are missing on either side; the same rows are simply bucketed into two more groups.

Limitations

We ran into the following limitations when performing the above benchmarks:

  • DuckDB SQL compatibility

Since the DuckDB storage engine executes queries in its own engine, the SQL syntax should be portable. A query that runs fine on InnoDB can fail on DuckDB when it uses a keyword or data type that DuckDB does not recognize. For example, the CAST function in MySQL accepts the UNSIGNED keyword, but when it’s pushed into DuckDB, it fails with the following error:

ERROR 7501 (HY000): [DuckDB] Catalog Error: Type with name UNSIGNED does not exist!
Did you mean "JSON"?.

Such queries need to be rewritten so DuckDB can process them. This can be automated with query-rewrite tools such as ProxySQL Query Rewrite feature or MySQL’s Rewriter Query Rewrite plugin, which we will cover in a separate blog post.

  • Collation

Unlike InnoDB, DuckDB does not apply the column collation and forces binary comparison. This can produce different result sets between engines.

For example, the following SELECT COUNT result set differs between DuckDB and InnoDB:

# DuckDB
mysql> SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM woocommerce.wp_wc_order_addresses WHERE address_type='billing' AND city<>'';
+----------------------+
| COUNT(DISTINCT city) |
+----------------------+
|               114412 |
+----------------------+
1 row in set (0.02 sec)

# InnoDB
mysql> SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM woocommerce.wp_wc_order_addresses WHERE address_type='billing' AND city<>'';
+----------------------+
| COUNT(DISTINCT city) |
+----------------------+
|               114375 |
+----------------------+
1 row in set (1.38 sec)

This is caused by DuckDB bypassing the column collation.

If we force binary comparison when running the query on InnoDB, we obtain the same result set as DuckDB:

# InnoDB BINARY
mysql> SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT BINARY city) FROM woocommerce.wp_wc_order_addresses WHERE address_type='billing' AND city<>'';
+-----------------------------+
| COUNT(DISTINCT BINARY city) |
+-----------------------------+
|                      114412 |
+-----------------------------+
1 row in set, 1 warning (1.34 sec)

To prevent this, group and join should be done on numeric IDs rather than text.

  • Decimals computed as Double

To improve performance, DuckDB does not support DECIMAL precision by default, so monetary columns are summed in floating point instead. This can lead to differences at sub-cent digits. If you need exact decimal values, you can disable the duckdb_use_double_for_decimal variable when importing the data.

We have not yet fully tested performance implications of disabling this, but we plan to cover this in another blogpost, in the near future.

  • Foreign keys

Traditionally in MySQL, cascaded foreign key operations such as ON DELETE CASCADE were handled internally by InnoDB, below the SQL layer, so they were not written to the binlog files.

Because the DuckDB storage engine does not perform these cascades itself, changes to child rows would be lost when replicating from InnoDB to DuckDB.

Starting with MySQL 9.6, foreign key cascades are handled at the SQL layer by default, so the affected rows are recorded in the binary log, making replication across different engines transparent.

The following MySQL blog post explains this change in detail:

https://blogs.oracle.com/mysql/no-more-hidden-changes-how-mysql-9-6-transforms-foreign-key-management

WooCommerce does not use cascading foreign keys, so this limitation does not apply in this case.

  • Observability

DuckDB exposes only a few of status variables. Status variables mostly show counters for statements (Com_duckdb_select, Com_duckdb_insert) and rows processed in batches.

InnoDB, by comparison, exposes dozens of status variables covering the buffer pool, I/O, row operations, and locking, and is instrumented in detail through the Performance Schema.

So there is little visibility into what the DuckDB engine is doing internally, such as memory use, disk spilling, or query execution, which makes monitoring and tuning harder than on InnoDB.

This gap makes sense though, given how much longer InnoDB has existed; DuckDB has had far less time to build equivalent instrumentation.

Why Columnar engine wins?

The reason is physical, and it comes down to how the data is stored on disk. InnoDB is a row store; it keeps all of a row’s columns together, which is ideal for transactional work, where you read or write an entire row at a time.

Analytics asks the opposite question. A report rarely needs the whole row; it sums one column, counts another, and groups by a third, across millions of rows.

In a row store, answering that means reading every full row from the B-tree and discarding most of it.

A columnar engine stores each column separately, so it reads only the fields a query touches, compresses them far better because the values share a type, and processes them in batches instead of row by row. Reading less, reading it in compressed form, and processing it in bulk is what turns InnoDB’s minutes into DuckDB’s seconds. The heavier the aggregation, the wider the gap, which is exactly what the benchmarks showed.

P.S. DuckDB is a potential solution for analytics use cases, and this post is part of our testing. At this time, Percona does not have a production DuckDB build and does not support it.
