posts.html:
Let’s say you’re processing events from an API into your CRM. An event comes in and tells you that a particular contact is a Director at a company. So you update the job title on their contact record in the CRM, along with some other fields like the company and whether they’re qualified.

A few seconds later, you receive another webhook telling you the same contact is a Manager at that company.

What’s happened here is that the second update was older than the first, but it took longer to arrive, and it has a different event ID.

This kind of thing is a big problem for GTM teams, because it affects how they segment, score and reach out to prospects.

The obvious thing to do to prevent things like this happening is to de-duplicate your webhooks – that is, make sure you’re not processing the same event twice.

However, this doesn’t help here.

Even though the handler was de-duplicating events, the second event still overwrote the information from the first.

To demonstrate the difference between the two methods, I’ve put together a small fixture in Python and Postgres. The two methods both de-duplicate events, and both process the database transactionally – the only difference is that the second one checks whether the contact revision in the incoming event is newer before it updates the CRM.

Note: this isn’t based on a real incident, or a real CRM – all records used here are synthetic.

Two different identities, two different guarantees

We’re modelling a scenario where an external data provider periodically sends complete snapshots of a set of data fields for each contact (in this case, company, job_title and lead_status). Each event contains a tenant ID, the name of the provider, a unique event ID, and the ID of the contact to which the data applies. The data from the event also includes a revision from the source.

We’re using Postgres and have two tables of interest:

  • inbound_events, with PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, provider, event_id), to answer “have we seen this event before?”
  • crm_contacts, with PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, provider, contact_id), to store the latest accepted snapshot for each contact.

The primary key on the first table lets us quickly determine whether we’ve seen an event before; the primary key on the second lets us find the contact the event concerns. But we also need a way to determine whether the snapshot in the event is more recent than what we have stored.

For this experiment, we’re assuming that the revision field contains a monotonically increasing integer, which we can trust to accurately reflect recency of the data from the provider. The provider might skip revisions, but if it sends us revision 10 and then revision 12, we know 12 represents the more recent state of the data in the source.

Arrival order Event ID Source revision Job title Lead status
First e10 10 Analyst new
Second e12 12 Director customer
Third e11 11 Manager qualified

Each event has a unique ID, so it represents a legitimate event to record. But when we receive e11, we already have revision 12 for the contact, so it would be incorrect to replace the existing data with the new (actually, older) data.

First, make deduplication work correctly

The following SQL is run in both cases to claim an event:

INSERT INTO inbound_events
    (tenant_id, provider, event_id, contact_id, source_revision, snapshot)
VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s)
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, provider, event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING event_id;

That SQL relies on the table’s primary key to prevent it from creating a new row. If the RETURNING clause yields no results, the existing event is read from the database and the contact ID, revision and snapshot are compared. The SQL includes %s placeholder strings, which are filled in by the psycopg driver.

That detail matters when two workers receive the same event concurrently. A unique-key conflict can force one worker to wait for the other’s transaction. After that wait, the handler reads the existing event in a separate statement rather than relying on an earlier statement snapshot.

PostgreSQL’s transaction isolation documentation explains why statement snapshots matter in this situation.

The important point is that the control implementation already has working deduplication. The comparison doesn’t depend on deliberately removing that protection.

The control: every new event updates the CRM

The control handler receives each new versioned event and unconditionally UPSERTs the contact. This is the ON CONFLICT part of its contact INSERT statement:

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, provider, contact_id) DO UPDATE SET
    source_revision = EXCLUDED.source_revision,
    company = EXCLUDED.company,
    job_title = EXCLUDED.job_title,
    lead_status = EXCLUDED.lead_status,
    last_applied_event = EXCLUDED.last_applied_event,
    application_count = crm_contacts.application_count + 1,
    updated_at = clock_timestamp()
RETURNING source_revision;

This works fine as long as the events are applied in source revision order, but what happens when they’re not? Let’s modify the test to insert events out of order, starting again with an empty database but this time inserting e10, e12, then e11. After e12, the contact is at revision 12 and has ExampleCo-12 / Director / customer from the enrichment store. When e11 arrives, the control contact handler accepts the event (it has a new event ID) and applies the UPSERT. The result?

Contact state after e11 Control handler
Source revision 11
Company ExampleCo-11
Job title Manager
Lead status qualified
Last applied event e11
Application count 3
Event outcome applied

Uh oh! The source revision has gone backwards from 12 to 11.

Nothing failed at the database level. The event had a valid identity, the transaction committed and the handler did exactly what its SQL instructed.

Yet, somehow the data in the CRM system was older than it had been the last time delivery had occurred.

The issue here is that while the uniqueness of the event tells us whether we’ve seen it before, it doesn’t tell a handler which order to apply updates to an entity in.

In order to fix this, it is necessary to ensure that an update only ever applies if the revision it represents is newer than the one currently held. The corrected code looks like this:

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, provider, contact_id) DO UPDATE SET
    source_revision = EXCLUDED.source_revision,
    company = EXCLUDED.company,
    job_title = EXCLUDED.job_title,
    lead_status = EXCLUDED.lead_status,
    last_applied_event = EXCLUDED.last_applied_event,
    application_count = crm_contacts.application_count + 1,
    updated_at = clock_timestamp()
WHERE EXCLUDED.source_revision > crm_contacts.source_revision
RETURNING source_revision;

EXCLUDED.source_revision is the revision proposed by the incoming event. crm_contacts.source_revision is the revision already stored.

If the incoming revision is higher, PostgreSQL applies the update.

If it’s equal or lower, the existing row isn’t updated. The handler can then inspect the current contact and event history to classify what happened.

Running the same sequence against this implementation produced a different outcome:

Contact state after e11 Unconditional control Revision-aware handler
Source revision 11 12
Company ExampleCo-11 ExampleCo-12
Job title Manager Director
Lead status qualified customer
Last applied event e11 e12
Application count 3 2
e11 outcome applied stale

Even though the event handler code was fixed to avoid replacing revision 12 with the older inbound event e11, it still attempted to apply e11 to the contact. However, since it didn’t succeed in replacing the contact revision, the contact’s application count, last applied event and updated_at timestamp were not affected.

The above state is the contact right after the first delayed event. It isn’t where the test ends. The test then applies yet another event with a different ID and the same old snapshot, e11-identical. The control applies that too, so it finishes at revision 11 with an application count of 4. The revision-aware handler records it as stale, so it stays at revision 12 with a count of 2.

What would happen if the workers were racing?

Although the above test scenario was useful for pinpointing the problem, in a real application, the webhooks would likely be processed by multiple workers concurrently.

It’s possible to do the revision comparison in the application code (Python), but then one has to be careful about the stored revision changing between reading it and sending the update to PostgreSQL.

The test fixture avoids this problem by performing the revision comparison in the database in the contact UPSERT statement. It tests the concurrent execution of event handlers by connecting to the database with different connections.

The test starts with a contact at revision 10:

  1. Worker A updates the contact to revision 12, then pauses after the contact UPSERT and before committing its transaction.
  2. Worker B tries to apply another event with revision 11 to the same contact.
  3. A third database connection observes what’s happening.

Instead of assuming that the workers are contending with each other, the test inspects the Postgres activity and lock information to see what’s going on:

SELECT pid, application_name, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE pid = ANY(%s)
ORDER BY pid;

The test also inspects pg_locks to see the corresponding transaction-ID locks.

Both times the test was run, it observed that one of the workers was indeed blocked by the other:

Observation Repetition 1 Repetition 2
Waiting worker’s event Lock / transactionid Lock / transactionid
pg_blocking_pids() Identified the revision 12 worker Identified the revision 12 worker
Transaction-ID locks Leader ExclusiveLock granted; follower ShareLock waiting Leader ExclusiveLock granted; follower ShareLock waiting
Final contact revision 12 12

In both runs, the revision 12 worker held a granted transaction-ID ExclusiveLock, while the other worker waited with an ungranted ShareLock on that transaction ID.

Once the revision 12 transaction committed, the waiting worker completed. Its revision 11 event was classified as stale.

The contact stayed at revision 12.

It was interesting to see that even though the stale UPSERT didn’t actually do anything, it still had to wait. The Postgres docs for INSERT ... ON CONFLICT explain that the conflicting row is locked before the update’s WHERE condition is evaluated, so there’s still some lock contention even if the conditional update is rejected.

It may seem pedantic, but it’s important to remember that the revision guard protects the state of the contact under the conditions tested. It doesn’t make concurrent updates free of locking.

Note: this was not intended as a benchmark, just something to work out if one worker would block the other and what state they were committed in.

Rollbacks, retries and contradictory revisions

Now, with the corrected handler:

What happened? Well, in the tests, after the UPSERT for the contact, but before the commit, an exception was injected. Due to the ACID properties of Postgres, that rolled back both the inbound event record and the mutation of the contact.

From an outside observer’s perspective, the contact was still the original one that had been committed. But when the event was retried, it was only applied once.

There was another test that checked what happened when an exception was thrown after the commit. In this case, the caller didn’t receive acknowledgement of the event.

In the database, the event had already been committed, and the contact had been created or updated. So, when the event was sent again, the contact wasn’t changed.

There’s a difference between throwing an exception before the commit and after the commit.

There is also a problem with two revisions from the same source being equal.

Two events with different event IDs that refer to the same revision of a contact may contain either (a) the same contact snapshot, in which case the second event is redundant (if it is for the current revision of the contact) or stale (if the contact has been revised further) unless it contradicts the retained revision history, or (b) different contact snapshots, in which case the two events present contradictory revision history from the provider.

The handler records a revision_conflict in the latter case and retains the previously accepted contact. It also checks for this when a contact is at a later revision but the events are retained in history. This way, it’s possible to identify when a provider contradicts itself at an older revision, even if the contact has moved on.

It does not, however, determine which of the two conflicting payloads is the true one – it’s a fixture to detect conflicts, not to resolve them.

There are tests for a few more things, including concurrent claims for the same event ID (and transaction rollback when that occurs), ensuring that events from different tenants or different providers don’t affect each other, handling of explicit null values when supplied in a complete snapshot, and handling of events that don’t provide a trustworthy revision.

The latter point is important: when an event is provided with no revision, the handler needs to record that it was seen but not alter the contact. It can’t assume that the event is newer or older than the existing contact merely because it’s arriving now.

Reproducing the experiment

The complete fixture can be found in a public repository: PostgreSQL CRM correctness under duplicate and out-of-order events.

The exact tested release commit is de003496.

The repository contains a Python handler, PostgreSQL schema, tests, pinned dependencies and a GitHub Actions workflow. It doesn’t include anything that would expose the handler as an HTTP endpoint for webhooks, or talk to a real CRM. It simulates the functions and database that are part of the fixture.

The fixture uses GitHub-hosted runners with temporary service containers for PostgreSQL, so there is no need to install it on a local machine.

It runs under the following environment:

Component Version
PostgreSQL server 17.11
Python 3.12.15
psycopg 3.3.6
pytest 9.1.1
Transaction isolation READ COMMITTED

A verified run on GitHub Actions executes two independent repetitions against fresh instances of the temporary PostgreSQL service.

Result Repetition 1 Repetition 2
Tests passed 85 85
Failures, errors or skips 0 0
Observed blocking cases 26 26

If you want to try to falsify this yourself and prove that it isn’t correct, you can re-run the experiment by forking this repo, turning on GitHub Actions in your fork, and manually running the CRM correctness experiment workflow, ensuring all four jobs complete successfully on the same commit (two each for PostgreSQL 17.11 and Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL 18). The jobs create some evidence which you can download, but it won’t be around for very long, so I’ve also attached the evidence from both runs to the v1.1.0 release along with checksums. The important bits from the evidence are what you see here, and also in the repo’s README.

Note: there was one tricky bit that required a bit of work while developing this. One of the earlier runs failed because the observation query was trying to sort on the Postgres transaction ID directly. That doesn’t work. But since the transaction ID was just used for sorting the results for display in the evidence, casting it to text was sufficient without changing anything about the processing or the assertions.

The results you see above were run after making that change.

Running it on Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL 18

I also ran the same tests against Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL 18.6.1, using the percona/percona-distribution-postgresql:18.6.1-3 image (pinned by digest in the workflow). This was run twice as well, on fresh instances, against commit 648beac (run 38931356745).

Result Repetition 1 Repetition 2
Tests passed 85 85
Failures, errors or skips 0 0
Observed blocking cases 26 26

The outcome was the same as on 17.11. The control still went back to revision 11, the revision-aware handler stayed at revision 12, and the waiting worker was blocked by the revision 12 worker before it came back as stale.

What this experiment does not prove

The revision guard depends on the contract on the events, namely:

  • The source provides revisions in a correct order. The revision must come from something that can correctly and reliably order the updates to a given contact. Merely comparing two integers does not inherently establish which of two pieces of information is more recent.
  • The snapshots provided in the events contain all the fields enriched by the source. If the source provides three fields, every accepted event must contain those three fields. If one of those fields should be cleared, the source must provide a value of null for that field. This doesn’t handle the case where different sources are providing partial snapshots that need to be merged.
  • Revision conflicts are detected, not reconciled. While the handler can detect when two snapshots with the same revision contain different information, and can ensure that a previously accepted snapshot is preserved, it has no way of determining which of the two payloads is correct.
  • An external CRM isn’t part of the PostgreSQL transaction. This experiment uses Postgres as the store for the contact information, which allows the handler to atomically commit the event and update the contact. If the update needed to be sent to an external API, the local PostgreSQL transaction alone couldn’t ensure that both operations happened atomically.
  • This doesn’t establish production correctness. These tests only test a few specific sequences of event delivery. They don’t prove that this approach is correct in all cases, that it will scale in a production environment, that it can handle all possible deadlocks, or that it will recover from all possible infrastructure problems.

Conclusion

What went wrong? By applying an old event that was provided with a new ID to our duplicate-safe event handler, we created a situation where Postgres was happy to apply the transaction and still maintain a consistent event history according to our event handler rules. This allowed an old event to overwrite our CRM contact, reverting it from revision 12 back to revision 11.

By adding a condition to our UPSERT to only apply the contact update if the event’s source revision is strictly higher than the one we already have, we can prevent this regression in all of the above scenarios. Interestingly, the concurrent scenarios still result in Postgres waiting on another transaction before returning.

This simple experiment illustrates two key questions we need to answer for an API-to-CRM workflow:

Have we processed this event before? – enforced by the event ID constraint.

Are we sure that this event contains newer information than what we already have? – enforced by trusting the ordering contract and only updating the CRM record if it is at a higher revision.

This experiment was built to illustrate the above point.

posts.excerpt: Percona Search for MongoDB 1.70.5-3 is now Generally Available and supported for production use. You can now easily run full-text, vector, and hybrid searches with automatic embedding on production Percona Server for MongoDB deployments. The release also adds the Hugging Face Inference API as a new automatic embedding provider.
posts.html:
Percona Search for MongoDB 1.70.5-3 is now Generally Available and supported for production use. You can now easily run full-text, vector, and hybrid searches with automatic embedding on production Percona Server for MongoDB deployments. The release also adds the Hugging Face Inference API as a new automatic embedding provider.

In this blog post, I cover why search now belongs next to the database, what held self-managed vector search back, what changed since the Technical Preview in August, and which parts of operations Percona tooling covers today and which come next.

Why semantic search matters to your database

Nowadays, people resign themselves to searching by exact keyword or document ID. They prefer to type what they mean, such as “orders that arrived damaged last month”, and expect results that match the intent even when the stored text uses different words. AI applications and agentic workflows even raise the stakes. For example, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline or an agent needs to retrieve context from your database before the model writes a response, but the model only sees the top handful of results. With MongoDB, this is much simpler. Running the retrieval inside MongoDB means there is no separate search database cluster to feed. Percona Search for MongoDB runs as a mongot search engine process alongside mongod and keeps your data and search indexes in sync through change streams.

What holds back self-managed vector search

While deployment is easy with MongoDB, we’ve found some challenges in adopting Vector Search in MongoDB production environments. That’s why we’ve decided to fork MongoDB’s mongot search engine into Percona Search for MongoDB and solve the following adoption walls:

Sovereignty

In MongoDB Vector Search Community and Enterprise Edition releases, automatic embedding is available only with Voyage AI models. Every document you index and every query your users type are sent to Voyage AI’s cloud to be converted into vectors. For support tickets, contracts, or patient notes held in a database you host yourself, that is often a dealbreaker. Moreover, air-gapped environments cannot use automatic embedding at all, and teams with data-residency obligations usually cannot either.

The bill

Hosted embedding is metered per token. You pay on every insert, update, search query, reranking, and chunking, so the cost grows with your data and your traffic, and changing models means paying to re-embed the whole corpus.

Operations

A lost search index can be rebuilt from mongod, but the index builds can take days. The faster path is a manual filesystem snapshot: stop mongot, copy its data directory, and restore it later. That snapshot has no scheduling, no point-in-time consistency with your database backup, and it becomes useless once it is older than your oplog window. The monitoring aspect is equally critical to vector search as it is to the database itself. For example, at 90% disk usage, mongot stops applying change events to existing indexes, so search serves stale results while the database reports healthy. Additionally, when there are no search indexes, the query returns no results, unlike traditional database indexing behavior. Without a monitoring and alerting system, your users will again be blind to silent failures.

Automatic embedding with your choice of model

At first, we’re solving the sovereignty wall and ease of use of automatic embeddings. mongot can generate embeddings for existing documents, update them as documents change, and embed the query text at search time. Your application sends plain text, and no one on your team needs to maintain a separate embedding pipeline that keeps vectors in step with the data.

Percona Search for MongoDB lets you pick where that inference runs. You can configure models from several providers on the same mongot instance, and the model named in each autoEmbed index decides which provider handles it.

We built this local-first. With a local OpenAI-compatible server or an in-cluster Hugging Face TEI model, document text stays inside your cluster and search works without outbound network access, so air-gapped deployments can use automatic embedding. There are no per-token charges on that path; the cost is the hardware you run the model on. You can also use the model that performs best in your language, or one your data science team fine-tuned.

Hosted providers stay available for teams that prefer them. Through OpenAI, Azure OpenAI and the Hugging Face Inference API you can reach more than 2,000 models, and Voyage AI remains supported. We plan to add more providers, and we intend to bring reranking with open cross-encoder models such as BAAI/bge-reranker-large after that.

What’s new in 1.70.5-3

Version 1.70.5-3 moves Percona Search for MongoDB from Technical Preview (1.70.3-1, August 2026) to General Availability. It is based on upstream mongot 1.70.5, so it includes the latest upstream fixes; the full list is in the MongoDB release notes.

Hugging Face Inference API as an embedding provider

The new HUGGINGFACE_INFERENCE provider joins VOYAGE and OPENAI_COMPATIBLE. It offers a hosted option for open embedding models without requiring you to run your own embedding server, providing you access to thousands of different models.

mongot calls the Hugging Face hf-inference feature-extraction pipeline, which serves open sentence embedding models such as BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5. It authenticates with your Hugging Face access token, sent as a bearer token. Setup steps are in Configure automatic embedding with the Hugging Face Inference API.

Running search with Percona tooling

Our goal is to enable you to operate the search tier using the same tools you already use for the database. Today, we already support Kubernetes deployment with our Operator. The next item on the roadmap is Backup and Monitoring.

License and support

Percona Search for MongoDB is free to use, with no paid edition, deployment limits or license-gated features. Like upstream mongot, it is published under the Server Side Public License (SSPL), which is source-available. You can read the code at github.com/percona/percona-mongot. If you need Percona Services (which is optional), contact us and we’ll happily cover your new search tier, along with Percona Server for MongoDB, the Operator, PBM, and PMM.

Get started and tell us what you need

To install, follow Install Percona Search for MongoDB. You may also want to play with our sample demo application.

We want to know which problems Percona Search for MongoDB solved for you, which embedding provider or model you need that we do not support yet, and where operating it was harder than it should be. Post on the Percona Search for MongoDB forum or talk to your Percona representative.

posts.excerpt: Most MongoDB replica sets start small. The working set fits in the WiredTiger cache, reads come from memory, and nobody thinks about disks. Then the data keeps growing. Orders, events and logs pile up for years, and one day the collection is ten times the size of the cache.
posts.html:
An alternative to sharding a MongoDB replica set that outgrew its memory: a proof of concept

A replica set that no longer fits in memory

Most MongoDB replica sets start small. The working set fits in the WiredTiger cache, reads come from memory, and nobody thinks about disks. Then the data keeps growing. Orders, events and logs pile up for years, and one day the collection is ten times the size of the cache.

From that point every read of a document that is not cached is a read from disk. Latency follows the disk, not the query. On the cluster I tested below, a read p95 of 70 ms was not a bad index, it was a disk at its IOPS limit.

The usual answer is sharding. It works, but it is a big step and very costly: a shard key you cannot easily change, mongos routers, config servers, balancing, and queries that need the shard key to stay fast. For a team whose real problem is “most reads are for recent data, and old data is in the way“, that is a lot of machinery.

The question I wanted to answer: can you keep the replica set you have, and put the recent data somewhere fast in front of it, without changing the application?

What Thermocline does

Thermocline is storage tiering for MongoDB. The cluster you have becomes the archive, exactly as it is. A new, smaller replica set in front of it holds the recent documents. The application connects to a proxy instead of the old cluster.

The application talks to one proxy; age decides which tier holds a document

Four pieces keep the two tiers consistent:

  1. The proxy speaks the MongoDB wire protocol. It sends a query to the fast tier when the fast tier can prove it holds the whole answer, and to the archive when it cannot. Writes go to the fast tier.
  2. The feeder reads the fast tier’s change stream and mirrors every write into the archive, so the archive always holds every document.
  3. The evictor removes documents from the fast tier once they are older than their collection’s age and the archive is confirmed to hold them.
  4. The warmer fills the fast tier from the archive with what is newer than that age.

Nothing is loaded by hand. The fast tier starts empty and fills from the warmer and from the documents that traffic requests.

How I measured it

The test cluster ran on Hetzner Cloud. It is built to be the case above, not a flattering one:

  • The existing cluster: a three-member replica set holding 40 million simulated orders, 47 GB of data. Each member was capped at 2.5 GB of memory (a 1 GB WiredTiger cache) and 3,000 reads per second on its data disk. That is a dataset roughly 47 times the cache.
  • The fast tier: a second three-member replica set, empty at the start.
  • The load: YCSB 0.17 with 64 threads, ten-minute runs, two runs per side. Each document carries a date spread over the past year, so “recent” means something.

Three mixes:

  • Online store: 85% reads, 10% updates, 5% inserts, with reads favouring the newest documents (YCSB’s latest distribution).
  1. Read-heavy: 95% reads, 5% updates, same distribution.
  2. Read-heavy, concentrated: 95% reads, 5% updates, with 99% of the activity on the newest 9% of the documents.

Every run was measured twice: the existing cluster alone, and the same cluster behind Thermocline. Same MongoDB release on both tiers, same caps, same client.

Results

The same capped cluster did 1.6x to 5.2x more operations per second behind Thermocline, with 0 operations refused in any run.

The more the traffic is about recent data, the bigger the gain: the concentrated mix went from 4,447 to 23,340 operations per second. Its read latency fell with it, from a p95 of 86 ms to 6 ms and a p99 of 92 ms to 8 ms.

At the same load, reads stop waiting for the disk. I asked both sides for 6,165 operations per second on the store mix, the old cluster’s maximum. Alone, it delivered 6,086 with a read p95 of 70.5 ms. Behind Thermocline it delivered 6,156 and 6,159 in two runs, with a read p95 of 2.8 ms and 2.1 ms. The p99 moved between 7 and 27 ms from one run to the next, against 81 ms alone. The archive’s disk did 1,838 reads per second instead of 2,704.

Adoption starts from an empty fast tier. The realistic first day is a fast tier with nothing in it, filled by traffic and the warmer. Over 30 minutes of the store mix, flat out, the pair averaged 8,221 operations per second, 42% more than the old cluster alone with cold caches (5,803). It passed the old cluster’s number after 100 seconds, averaged 6,417 in the first five minutes and 9,146 in the last five, and copied 271,271 documents up from the archive on the way.

Where it does not help

The gain comes from reads that the fast tier can answer. Everything else still lands on the existing cluster, and that sets the limits:

  • Writes still reach the archive. Every write is mirrored to the existing cluster, and mirroring an update means the archive reads that document from disk first. In the store mix, updates ran at the old cluster’s speed, and the update p99 was higher than alone (455 to 472 ms against 104 to 189 ms). I am working on that tail now.
  • Reads of old data are as slow as before. A query that reaches past what the fast tier holds goes to the archive. If your reads are spread evenly over all of history, there is little to gain.
  • Both tiers must run the same MongoDB release. The archive answers the application’s own queries, so it has to understand them. Adopting an older cluster means upgrading it first.
  • It is a proof of concept. It has an extensive test suite, but it has not run in production. Do not point real traffic at it yet.

The gain depends on the mix: 1.6x on the store mix and 5.2x when activity is concentrated on recent data, on the same hardware. Measure your own case before believing mine.

Why it matters

A replica set that outgrew its memory usually gets one of two answers: bigger machines, or sharding. Both cost money and time, and sharding changes how the application has to be written. Tiering is a third option for the common case where most of the traffic is about recent data: keep the cluster you have as the archive, put a small fast cluster in front of it, and let age decide where each document lives.

The code is on GitHub atgithub.com/zelmario/thermocline, under the Apache 2.0 license, and its README explains how to run it.

If you have a replica set in this situation, I would like to hear about it, and even more about a workload where this does not work. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Note: This is a proof of concept. Thermocline is a POC I built to answer one question: can a small fast cluster in front of an existing replica set take the load off it, without changing the application, so that sharding or bigger servers are not the only way out?

The results say it can be a viable alternative for the right workload. The numbers come from a test cluster. It has not run in production yet.

posts.excerpt: Every MySQL schema that’s been around for a few years collects indexes nobody remembers adding. Some were for a report that was retired. Some came from an ORM migration. A few were added “just in case” and never used. They all cost something: extra writes on every INSERT and UPDATE, increased buffer pool pressure, larger backups, and slower schema changes.
posts.html:
Every MySQL schema that’s been around for a few years collects indexes nobody remembers adding. Some were for a report that was retired. Some came from an ORM migration. A few were added “just in case” and never used. They all cost something: extra writes on every INSERT and UPDATE, increased buffer pool pressure, larger backups, and slower schema changes.

MySQL makes it look easy to find them. Since 5.7, the sys schema ships a view called sys.schema_unused_indexes, and one query gives you a list of indexes with zero reads since the server started. It’s tempting to turn that list straight into DROP INDEX statements.

In an earlier post, How to Find Duplicate, Unused, and Invisible Indexes in MySQL, I showed how to use that view on a single server. This post covers what that approach misses once replicas are involved.

I’ve seen that go wrong, and it’s why I wrote check_unused_indexes. It’s a small Python script that asks the same question on every server in a replication topology and only reports an index when the answer is “unused” everywhere. This post covers why that matters, how the tool works, and how I’d use it on a production system.

Why one server’s answer isn’t enough

sys.schema_unused_indexes is built on Performance Schema’s per-index I/O counters. Those counters are local to the server you query. They know nothing about what your replicas are doing.

That’s the trap. In most setups, the primary takes writes and the light OLTP reads, while the heavy reads go elsewhere:

  • A reporting replica runs month-end queries that lean on an index the application never touches.
  • An Aurora reader serves the dashboard traffic, so the writer never sees those lookups.
  • In a Galera or Percona XtraDB Cluster, the load balancer may send one kind of query to one node more than the others.

So an index can show zero reads on the primary and still be the only thing keeping a replica’s reporting query under a second. Drop it on the primary, the DDL replicates, and the replica falls over into a full table scan.

There’s a second catch. The counters reset when MySQL restarts. A server patched on Tuesday has seen only a few days of traffic. A weekly batch job or a quarterly report hasn’t run yet, so its indexes look unused when they aren’t.

How check_unused_indexes works

You give the script a list of servers and tell it which one is the primary. It determines which of those servers belong to that primary’s topology, collects the unused-index lists from each one, and keeps only the indexes that appear on every list. It runs in three steps.

check_unused_indexes · 3 steps, 2 abort points

If the script can’t get a complete answer from every node, it stops instead of printing a list it can’t stand behind.

Step 1: discover the topology. The script connects to every server in your inventory and reads a little metadata from each:

  • SHOW REPLICA STATUS (or SHOW SLAVE STATUS on older versions) for the source host and port
  • @@wsrep_cluster_name, to spot Galera and PXC cluster members
  • information_schema.replica_host_status, which only exists on Aurora
  • the Uptime status variable

Then it walks downstream from the primary. A replica whose source matches the primary’s address is pulled in, then that replica’s own replicas, and so on. Chained and circular replication are handled the same way. If a node is in a Galera cluster, all its cluster peers are included as well. Aurora readers are matched by server ID, or by an alias naming convention I’ll come back to later.

Servers in the inventory that don’t belong to this primary are left out. That means you can keep a single inventory file for the entire fleet and point the script to different primaries.

Step 2: ask every node. For each node in the resolved topology, the script queries sys.schema_unused_indexes. Two filters apply on every node:

  • System schemas (sys, mysql, performance_schema, information_schema) are always skipped.
  • Any index whose first column is part of a foreign key is excluded. MySQL needs an index on FK columns, and it won’t let you drop one that a constraint depends on. Even if it did, you wouldn’t want to.

You can narrow things further with –include-schema and –include-table, or skip more schemas with –ignore-schema.

Step 3: intersect. The script starts with the primary’s list and removes anything that isn’t also on every other node’s list. What’s left is the set of indexes with zero reads everywhere the script looked. It prints that as a table, followed by the DDL to run on the primary.

Getting started

The script is a single file. It needs Python 3.6 or newer and one library, pymysql.

git clone https://github.com/Percona-Lab/check_unused_indexes.git
cd check_unused_indexes
pip3 install --user pymysql

Credentials come from a MySQL option file. By default that’s ~/.my.cnf, and you can point at another one with -c:

[client]
user=index_audit
password=change_me

The account needs to read sys.schema_unused_indexes and information_schema, and to run SHOW REPLICA STATUS. Use the same user on every node. The script reads only and never changes anything on the servers.

There are two ways to tell the script about your servers. For a quick check, you can list them on the command line:

python3 check_unused_indexes.py \
  --primary "db-primary=10.0.0.10:3306" \
  --replicas "db-replica-1=10.0.0.11:3306,db-replica-2=10.0.0.12:3306"

For anything bigger, I’d use an inventory file. It’s one alias=host:port per line. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored, and the port defaults to 3306 if you leave it off.

# inventory.txt
db-primary=10.0.0.10:3306
db-replica-1=10.0.0.11:3306
db-replica-2=10.0.0.12:3306
db-analytics=10.0.0.13:3306

Then pass the primary’s alias:

python3 check_unused_indexes.py --inventory inventory.txt --primary db-primary

One thing to check before your first run: the topology walk matches each replica’s Source_Host against the addresses in your inventory, as plain strings. If your replicas were set up with CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST=’db-primary.internal’, put that same hostname in the inventory, not the IP. If the topology comes back with fewer nodes than you expect, this is almost always why.

A run, step by step

Here’s what a run looks like against the inventory above, with the primary and two replicas reachable. The db-analytics server in the file replicates from a different primary, so the topology walk excludes it. This is the example output from the project README, with the colours stripped.

=== Step 1: Discovering Topology ===
Mapping topology downstream from Primary: db-primary...

Resolved Topology (3 nodes): db-primary, db-replica-1, db-replica-2

=== Step 2: Checking Unused Indexes on Nodes ===
Checking [PRIMARY] db-primary (10.0.0.10:3306) - Uptime: 42.1 days
  └─ Found 12 unused index candidates on this node.
Checking [REPLICA/CLUSTER] db-replica-1 (10.0.0.11:3306) - Uptime: 42.1 days
  └─ Found 8 unused index candidates on this node.
Checking [REPLICA/CLUSTER] db-replica-2 (10.0.0.12:3306) - Uptime: 14.0 days
  └─ Found 5 unused index candidates on this node.

=== Step 3: Intersecting Unused Indexes Across Topology ===

Safe Target Indexes (Unused across ALL 3 checked nodes):
================================================================================
SCHEMA               | TABLE                          | INDEX NAME
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
app_db               | orders                         | idx_legacy_status
app_db               | users                          | idx_created_at
================================================================================

Total Candidate Indexes: 2

Generated DDL Statements (Execute on Primary):
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ALTER TABLE `app_db`.`orders` ALTER INDEX `idx_legacy_status` INVISIBLE;
ALTER TABLE `app_db`.`users` ALTER INDEX `idx_created_at` INVISIBLE;
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Look at the numbers in Step 2. Run the sys query on the primary alone and you get 12 indexes to drop. Only 2 of those 12 are unused on both replicas. The other 10 are carrying read traffic somewhere, and dropping them would have hurt.

That gap between 12 and 2 is the whole point of the tool. Expect a gap like this on most real systems. Replicas exist precisely to take the load the primary doesn’t serve.

If you only want the DDL, for a ticket or a change request, add -qs (–quiet-summary) to skip the table.

Safety checks: what happens when a node is down

The intersection is only as good as its inputs. If a replica can’t be reached and the script quietly skips it, the result looks complete but isn’t. Any index that replica depends on could end up on the drop list. The latest version therefore refuses to guess.

SituationWhat the script does
Primary can’t be reached in Step 1Stops with a fatal error. Without the primary there’s no topology to walk.
Some inventory nodes can’t be reached in Step 1Prints a connection warning naming each one, with a note that they weren’t evaluated.
Primary drops out during Step 2Stops at once. There’s nothing to intersect against.
A replica or cluster peer drops out during Step 2Stops with a fatal error and lists the nodes, unless you pass–force.
Same, with–forceCarries on with the nodes that answered, prints a warning, and labels the result “checked nodes”.
A node’s uptime is under the thresholdFinishes, then warns that its statistics may be incomplete. The default is 7 days; change it with-u, or set 0 to disable it.

The Step 1 warning needs an explanation. If a replica is already down when you start, the script can’t read its replication status. It has no way of knowing that the node belongs to this topology, so it can’t treat it as missing. All it can do is tell you which inventory entries it couldn’t reach. Read that warning before you trust the result.

–force is there for the case where you know a node is gone for good, such as a replica being decommissioned. Don’t use it to get past a network blip.

The last option is –pause-seconds, which waits between Step 1 and Step 2. It’s meant for testing these checks. Start a run with –pause-seconds 60, stop MySQL on one replica while it waits, and check that the script aborts:

python3 check_unused_indexes.py -i inventory.txt -p db-primary –pause-seconds 60; echo “exit=$?”

You should see FATAL ERROR: Failed to inspect index state on resolved replica/peer node(s) and an exit code of 1. Run it once on a test setup before you rely on it in production.

From candidate list to dropped index

The script prints DDL and stops there. It never runs anything for you, and that’s on purpose. The list is a set of candidates to review, not a set of orders.

By default, the DDL makes the index invisible rather than dropping it:

ALTER TABLE app_db.users ALTER INDEX idx_created_at INVISIBLE;

Invisible indexes arrived in MySQL 8.0. The optimizer stops using the index, but MySQL continues to maintain it on every write. Making it invisible is a metadata change, and so is undoing it, so rolling back takes seconds. A real DROP INDEX followed by a re-create means rebuilding the index, which on a large table can take hours.

This is the rollout I’d follow:

  1. Run the script and read the candidate list yourself. Make sure every name makes sense to you.
  2. Run the INVISIBLE statements on the primary. They replicate, so every node in the topology changes.
  3. Wait through at least one full business cycle, including the month-end jobs and any weekly batch. Watch the slow query log and your query metrics for regressions.
  4. If something slows down, run ALTER INDEX … VISIBLE on that index, and you’re back where you started.
  5. Once you’re confident, drop the indexes. –action drop prints the DROP INDEX statements, and –action both prints both kinds.

One more thing before step 5. On MySQL 8.0 you can set use_invisible_indexes=on in optimizer_switch for a single session. That lets you check whether a query you’re unsure about would still pick the index, without making it visible to the application.

For a longer walkthrough of invisible indexes, including testing a single query with SET_VAR(optimizer_switch = ‘use_invisible_indexes=on’), see my earlier post.

Options at a glance

OptionWhat it doesDefault
-p,–primaryPrimary alias from the inventory, oralias=host:port/host:portrequired
-r,–replicasComma-separated replica specs on the command linenone
-i,–inventoryInventory file, onealias=host:portper linenone
-c,–configMySQL option file with credentials~/.my.cnf
-u,–min-uptimeWarn when a node has been up fewer days than this7
–actionDDL to print:invisible,droporbothinvisible
-s,–include-schemaOnly check these schemasall
-t,–include-tableOnly check these tablesall
–ignore-schemaExtra schemas to skip, on top of the system onesnone
-qs,–quiet-summaryPrint only the DDLoff
–forceContinue if a replica fails in Step 2 (unsafe)off
–pause-secondsWait between Step 1 and Step 2, for testing0
–colorauto,alwaysorneverauto

Limits worth knowing

No tool can see traffic that hasn’t happened yet, and this one is no exception. Keep these in mind:

  • Only servers in the inventory are checked. A replica you forgot to list is invisible to the script, and so is everything it serves.
  • Unique indexes can still show up. sys.schema_unused_indexes excludes primary keys, but not UNIQUE indexes. A unique index can have zero reads and still be enforcing a business rule. Check every candidate with SHOW CREATE TABLE before you drop it.
  • Statistics start at the last restart. The uptime warning helps, but you decide what “long enough” means for your workload.
  • Performance Schema must be on. It’s on by default. If someone turned it off, the sys view has nothing to report.
  • Aurora needs an alias convention. Readers are matched by server ID or by alias prefix. Name the writer aurora and the readers aurora-reader-1, aurora-reader-2 and so on, and they’ll be grouped correctly.
  • Hosts are matched as strings. As covered above, use the same host name or IP in the inventory as the replicas use in Source_Host.
  • It finds unused indexes, not duplicate ones. An index can be redundant even if another index covers the same columns. For those, run pt-duplicate-key-checker from Percona Toolkit, as described in the earlier post.

Try it and tell me what breaks

The project is on GitHub at Percona-Lab/check_unused_indexes under the Apache 2.0 license. It’s one Python file, so it’s easy to read before you run it against anything that matters, and I’d encourage you to do so.

If it misreads your topology, or you run something it doesn’t handle yet (group replication, multi-source replicas), please open an issue or send a pull request. Real topologies are messier than test labs, and those reports are how the tool gets better.

posts.excerpt: I would like to introduce here the curious case that I had on a Patroni Cluster in production, after a migration from Oracle, with timezone differences between what was written from an application log and what was set in PostgreSQL.
posts.html:
I would like to introduce here the curious case that I had on a Patroni Cluster in production, after a migration from Oracle, with timezone differences between what was written from an application log and what was set in PostgreSQL.

First of all a quick description of our setup. We have a two nodes Patroni cluster on Open Stack virtual machines, PostgreSQL 18, with leader and a read only replica, so we write only on one node and use the second for data extractions. All applications use Kubernetes pods that are also setup in Open Stack and access PostgreSQL via PgBouncer connection pooler. We do have also some Java application making use of their own Hikari connection pooler. All on premises.

The application, being a legacy one, needed to use all the time data types in the timezone of the customer, so I had to setup the timezone of the PostgreSQL cluster different from the one of the VMs, that is in UTC. That was the first error as I set it up using a simple ALTER SYSTEM SET TIMEZONE followed by a SELECT pg_reload_conf(). This changes the timezone on the postgresql.auto.conf configuration file, which is totally good if you have a normal single node or replica PostgreSQL but not with a Patroni Cluster! I will return on this point in a moment.

In itself the migration was fine, but we had to tailor a little bit the resources assigned to the nodes as unfortunately we were not able to test, prior to the migration, some parts of the application. So we had to increase RAM on the VMs and modify shared_buffers parameter, doing a restart of the PostgreSQL cluster one node at a time.

Unfortunately the restart wiped out the timezone configuration that I did, as I should have added this through a patronictl edit-config command as I did for the shared_buffers. At least we recognized quickly the problem as the timezone of the whole Patroni Cluster reverted back to UTC. This time I changed it modifying the Patroni Cluster configuration, using the following patronictl command edit-config:

Fig. 1 – patronictl edit-config command

And adding the correct timezone:

Fig. 2 – Result of edit-config command

Confirmed issuing a show-config:

Fig. 3 – Result of show-config command

After that we resumed normal operations and all seemed fine, problem solved, no big issue or disruptions to our customer.

The day after I got contacted by one developer telling me that PostgreSQL in production is still in UTC. I checked it immediately and it was instead in WAT, confirmed issuing:

Fig. 4 – Screenshot of show timezone in pgAdmin

Then the developers sent me the results of a query done on an application log table showing a clear inconsistency of timestamps, some were correct and some with UTC timezone! That is a very bad scenario, where you do not have a clear indication, all wrong or all correct, but mixed results.

I started suspecting that there was something wrong on the application side as all that I saw on the database was correct, except some of the values that were recorded. So my next move was to ask devops to restart one by one all the application pods (remember that we are using Kubernetes).

This action brought mixed results as at the beginning it seemed that problem was solved and no rows with timestamp with wrong timezone was inserted…but after some time the first rows with UTC started resurfacing again! That was weird so I started digging a little bit more and searched our setup and our structure, as I was sure that the PostgreSQL database in itself was not the culprit.

As you may have guessed at this point there was one Elephant in the room that I had not yet investigated (and no was not PostgreSQL Elephant, AKA Slonik): PgBouncer! In fact I had totally left out of the picture the connection pooler as I thought that it was installed in kubernetes as a sidecar of the application pods, so expecting that a restart of the pods would have affected also PgBouncer.

As that was the architectural schema that was decided some years ago for our applications. Turned out that this was not the case!

Let’s make a quick excursus on why it is extremely important to have a connection pooler in PostgreSQL, the pool mode parameter of PgBouncer and the possible ways of installing and configuring it. These points are important to understand our case.

PostgreSQL connections are costly, mainly in terms of RAM, so much that there is a parameter max_connections to limit the maximum number of sessions, both active and idle. The default value is 100 which obviously is quite low, but rising it means that we need to ensure that we have enough RAM available, as the overhead for each connection is roughly 10 Mb. Bringing this parameter up for example to 500 means having already 5 Gb of RAM used just for idle connections, without even issuing any query!

Here is where connection poolers come to the rescue, as they are capable of recycling the connections, so that applications do not need to open a new connection each time they need to query the database. The pool maintains a fixed set of open connections, all requests borrow a connection, use it, and return it to the pool. The connection itself is never closed between requests, it stays open and ready so that the next request picks it up instantly.

PgBouncer is the de facto standard for connection pooling in PostgreSQL as it is lightweight, easy to configure and maintain. There is a very important setup choice to be made when installing PgBouncer: the pool mode, that decides the behaviour of the pooler. There are 3 possible choices: Session – Transaction – Statement.

Session Pooling: Assigns a server connection to a client as soon as it connects and holds it until the client disconnects. It acts almost like a direct connection to PostgreSQL, supporting all session features, but offers the least connection reuse. This is the most safe way to configure PgBouncer, and since we use some session features like Prepared Statements, this was our choice.

Transaction Pooling: Assigns a server connection only for the duration of a single BEGIN … COMMIT/ROLLBACK transaction. Once the transaction completes, the connection goes back to the pool for another client to use.

Statement Pooling: Assigns a server connection for a single SQL statement, returning it immediately after execution. It allows maximum reuse, but breaks multi-statement transactions (BEGIN … COMMIT) and session features.

One last word on what are the recommended ways to install PgBouncer: first of all it should be on a separate server respect the PostgreSQL cluster, then in a Kubernetes environment, such as ours, it can be installed as a sidecar to Kubernetes pods (which is the recommended way for most cases) or as a separate deployment in its own pod. Turns out that we had installed PgBouncer in this last way instead of having it in the same pod of the application.

Now that we have a complete picture, let’s go back to our case. Since our PgBouncer was installed as a standalone pod and not in sidecar, this become my primary culprit, searching a little bit I found out that there is the possibility in PgBouncer that if a database is created or its timezone is altered via ALTER DATABASE … SET timezone, PgBouncer does not properly invalidate its internal startup-parameter cache.

In our case the timezone was changed through Patroni, not ALTER DATABASE, but PgBouncer still kept a stale cached TimeZone.

So when a connection is recycled:

  • PostgreSQL natively sets the timezone to Africa/Lagos.
  • PgBouncer looks at its cached baseline state for that database/user profile from when it first booted up (which was reset to UTC when we restarted the Patroni nodes remember!).
  • PgBouncer then subtly injects a session-level override back to the client, effectively masking the database’s actual default settings.

It was exactly our case, as the restart of Patroni Cluster nodes returned all the system to UTC, then we modified it again to WAT, but we never restarted the PGBouncer pod, so we still had some sessions in the pool with UTC timezone. That explained also the mix between correct and wrong timezones in the timestamps, it depended from the session with which the row was inserted, if it was one of the old ones we had UTC.

The fix at this point was obvious: clear the cache of PgBouncer. This can be done with a simple restart of that pod or a reload of the configuration. In our case we restarted PgBouncer and surely this action solved all our timezone problems as from that point we had only timestamps with correct timezone, confirming the above scenario.

So this was the curious case of timezone inconsistencies between PostgreSQL and PgBouncer, in the end was easily solved and not disruptive, it was due mainly to a couple of errors and assumptions that I did and that were surely avoidable, that’s why I wanted to bring attention to this subject: prevent others doing my errors and recognize faster the issue.

Summarizing all in a few key points of lessons learned:

  • After changing timezone in Patroni, always restart or RECONNECT PgBouncer so the pool doesn’t keep stale session settings.
  • Remember to always change timezone in a Patroni cluster using patronictl command edit-config and not ALTER SYSTEM SET TIMEZONE.
  • In a Kubernetes environment install PgBouncer as a sidecar to Kubernetes pods instead of a standalone pod.

Hope it will help some of you!

This post is part of the Percona Community Writers Program.

posts.excerpt: PostgreSQL community images address a real gap in how a Kubernetes database operator earns your trust. Running a database operator on Kubernetes means trusting two things: the code, and the container images the operator pulls. The code is on GitHub, easy to inspect, easy to fork…
posts.html:
PostgreSQL community images address a real gap in how a Kubernetes database operator earns your trust. Running a database operator on Kubernetes means trusting two things: the code, and the container images the operator pulls. The code is on GitHub, easy to inspect, easy to fork. The container images, the registry that hosts them, and the license that governs them all sit with the vendor, and any of those three can change without the source repository changing at all. Starting with Percona Operator for PostgreSQL 3.0.0, you can run the operator against community images you build yourself from the official PostgreSQL packages on download.postgresql.org, in a registry you control.

TL;DR

  • Community Docker Images: tech preview in PGO 3.0.0, official in 3.1.0. Point the operator at upstream-built PostgreSQL images instead of the Percona Distribution images.
  • Build them yourself from the official PostgreSQL source. The Dockerfiles pull packages from download.postgresql.org (the PGDG repositories), so the trust chain runs from PGDG to your registry with no vendor in the middle.
  • There are limits. Anything Percona-specific (TDE in our distribution build, for example) does not exist in an upstream-built image. That trade is intentional.

In this post:

  • How open source gets diluted in practice
  • Why distributions exist anyway, honestly
  • How Community Docker Images work
  • Limits of the upstream path
  • What to try, what to tell us

How open source gets diluted

Open source has changed in the last few years, and not always for the better. Companies have learned that you can keep a project’s source code fully open and still capture most of the lock-in by quietly closing the parts that matter in production: the release artifacts, the container images, the supported OS list, the certified Kubernetes distributions, the marketplace listings.

Same project, closed artifacts

You can have a fully community CNCF project that does not appear on the Red Hat Marketplace except as a paid Enterprise edition. Similarly, you can have a vendor that ships one packaging in the community and a richer one in Enterprise with the features you actually need in production. The license still says “open source.” The practical experience says “you depend on us.” And the source repository’s license is not the only license that matters here: a vendor can change the license, the trademark policy, or the distribution terms on the container images alone, while leaving the source repository untouched. That has happened in the PostgreSQL operator space recently, and the community noticed.

Why the community is right to be wary

Nobody outside the vendor can predict when a license will change, when a feature will move behind a paywall, or when an external contribution will get rejected because it competes with an Enterprise feature. Recent history has plenty of examples and the PostgreSQL community has been paying attention. When this community resists vendor-controlled distributions, it is not nostalgia. It is a rational read of where things have gone before.

I work on Percona’s PostgreSQL operator, so I see this conversation from the vendor side. The skepticism is fair. The honest question for us is what to do about it.

Why distributions exist anyway

Acknowledging the community’s concerns does not mean distributions are pointless. There are real reasons to ship one, and pretending otherwise makes for bad blog posts.

What a distribution buys you

A vendor-built distribution lets the vendor:

  1. Control the build process, dependencies, and defaults so they fit a specific user shape.
  2. Ship hotfixes faster, because the whole release path sits in one place.
  3. Fork PostgreSQL itself when something the upstream community will not accept, or can take years to accept, matters to customers, such as Transparent Data Encryption.
  4. For a Kubernetes operator, ship images with exactly the tools and extensions the operator supports, and skip everything else. The CVE surface stays smaller.
  5. Give QA and Service teams a predictable environment. “We support extensions A, B, C and not D, X, Z” is only honest if QA actually exercises A, B, C and the Service team can work with them in the production environment.
  6. Give customers one accountable party for the full release cycle, from hotfix through package availability. Some teams explicitly need that contract for compliance and audit reasons.
  7. And yes, less positive reasons that we covered above also apply, which is exactly the part the community keeps pointing at.

The trade-off you accept

If you run the vendor distribution, you accept that the vendor’s registry, image policy, and supported-extension matrix become part of your stack. If the vendor changes any of that, your operator deployment changes with it. That is not hypothetical for users who have lived through it on other products.

So the real question is whether you can keep the benefits a distribution provides for the users who want them, while leaving an honest, supported door open for users who do not. That is the door PGO 3.0.0 opens.

Community PostgreSQL Images in PGO 3.0.0

Starting with Percona Operator for PostgreSQL 3.0.0, the operator can run against images built from upstream PostgreSQL packages, not just the Percona Distribution images. This is what we are calling Community PostgreSQL Images. In 3.0.0, the feature ships as a tech preview. In 3.1.0, these images become part of our official release cycle and are fully documented.

One of the main advantages of Community Docker Images is that the community can request or contribute any extension that does not exist in the official Percona PostgreSQL distribution. TimescaleDB and Citus are the first examples: the community asked for them, and we shipped both in the Community Images set from day one.

How to use “Community PostgreSQL images”

The operator does not care where the image came from, as long as the image meets the operator’s runtime expectations

A typical CR using a community image looks like this:

apiVersion: pgv2.percona.com/v2
kind: PerconaPGCluster
metadata:
  name: cluster1
spec:
  image: registry.example.com/postgresql-community:18
  postgresVersion: 18
  proxy:
    pgBouncer:
      image: registry.example.com/pgbouncer-community:1.23
  backups:
    pgbackrest:
      image: registry.example.com/pgbackrest-community:2.51
  # other spec fields unchanged from a normal CR

The fields that change are spec.image, spec.proxy.pgBouncer.image, and spec.backups.pgbackrest.image. You can build and publish all three images under your own registry, with your own tags if that helps you track versions. The operator drives the rest of the deployment the same way it always has: instances, backups, replication, monitoring, all of it.

What ships are in each image

Each Community Docker Image is a thin layer over the chosen base (UBI9 or UBI8) plus the packages the operator needs for that role. Where you see {N}, substitute the PostgreSQL major you build for (17, 18, and so on).

postgres image (e.g. postgres17):

Package Role
postgresql{N}-server PostgreSQL server
postgresql{N}-contrib contrib modules
pg_repack_{N} online table/index reorganization
pgaudit_{N} audit logging
set_user_{N} privilege escalation control
pgvector_{N} vector similarity search
wal2json_{N} WAL to JSON logical decoding
pg_cron_{N} in-database cron scheduler
pgbackrest</code> backup/restore tool
patroni HA cluster manager
timescaledb-2-postgresql-{N} time-series extension (x86_64 only; EL9 only for PG18)
citus_{N} distributed PostgreSQL (PG16+ only)

pgbackrest image:

Package Role
pgbackrest backup/restore tool only

pgbouncer image:

Package Role
pgbouncer connection pooler only

The split is intentional. The postgres image ships the full operator-aware runtime. The backup and proxy images stay minimal. As a result, the operator’s components are in separate failure domains and shrink the attack surface of each container.

Limits worth being honest about

A community image is not a Percona Distribution image. Two practical consequences:

  • Distribution-only features will not work. Transparent Data Encryption, for example, lives in the Percona Distribution build. A community image built from upstream PostgreSQL does not include it. If you depend on TDE, run the distribution image.
  • Support boundaries are different. Percona Support is responsible for the Percona Distribution images and the operator code. A community image you built yourself

Ultimately, these are the right trade-offs. The point of community images is to give you transparency and control. Taking care of your own image is part of that deal. At the same time, we publish all three images under perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator on Docker Hub so you can evaluate the tech preview without standing up your own build pipeline first. perconalab is Percona’s non-production namespace, so use those images for testing. For production, build and sign your own.

UBI9 (EL9):

docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-postgres14-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-postgres15-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-postgres16-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-postgres17-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-postgres18-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-pgbackrest-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-pgbouncer-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-upgrade-community

UBI8 (EL8):

docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-ubi8-postgres14-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-ubi8-postgres15-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-ubi8-postgres16-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-ubi8-postgres17-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-ubi8-postgres18-community
docker.io/perconalab/percona-postgresql-operator:main-ubi8-upgrade-community

How to build the images

The Dockerfile, the package list, and a sample CI job ship in percona-docker/postgresql-containers/community. The build is a regular make target on top of docker buildx, so you can run it on any multi-platform builder.

# Prerequisites: docker buildx with a multi-platform builder
docker buildx create --use --name multiarch

# Build and push all PostgreSQL community images (UBI9 / EL9)
git clone https://github.com/percona/percona-docker
cd percona-docker/postgresql-containers/community
make all TAG=1.0.0 REGISTRY=myrepo/percona-postgresql-operator

# Or a single image
make postgres17 TAG=1.0.0 REGISTRY=myrepo/percona-postgresql-operator

# UBI8 / EL8 variants
make all-ubi8 TAG=1.0.0-ubi8 REGISTRY=myrepo/percona-postgresql-operator

make all builds all three images (postgres, pgBouncer, pgBackRest) so they stay version-aligned. Override REGISTRY and TAG to point at your own namespace and tagging scheme. Once the images are in your registry, plug them into the CR fields shown earlier, and the operator picks them up.

Full build documentation: percona-docker/postgresql-containers/community/README.md.

How to contribute

Community images live in percona/percona-docker, and the build is driven by a transform.py generator that produces the Dockerfiles under build/. The files under build/ are regenerated on every sync, so contributions go through the generator, never through the generated files.

Full contribution guide: community/CONTRIBUTING.md.

How to provide feedback

Two channels, depending on the shape of the feedback:

  • GitHub issue on percona/percona-postgresql-operator with the community-images label. Use this for bug reports, missing extensions, build problems, and concrete requests. The label keeps all community-image reports in one filter the team watches.

What’s next

The first step was taking full engineering ownership of Percona Operator for PostgreSQL as an independent project, so the roadmap, the release cadence, and the governance live with one team that the community can talk to directly. Community PostgreSQL Images are the next step in that same commitment. If the community adopts this path, we have ideas for what to invest in next.

We will let the community tell us. If this is useful, we keep investing here. We are ready to add more features to the operator around Community Images. Conversely, if nobody adopts it, that is also a signal, and an honest one.

Try the tech preview in 3.0.0. Open an issue if the build flow is rougher than it should be. Tell us what you want next on the forum or directly on GitHub.

Try It Out

  • Percona Operator for PostgreSQL docs: https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/percona/percona-postgresql-operator
  • Community Forum: https://forums.percona.com, share your feedback, ask questions, or report issues

posts.excerpt: Many MySQL configurations inherit redo log sizing from defaults, aging blog posts, or configuration folklore.
posts.html:
Introduction

Many MySQL configurations inherit redo log sizing from defaults, aging blog posts, or configuration folklore.

innodb_redo_log_capacity gets set once… and then quietly fades into the background.

But redo log capacity directly shapes how efficiently MySQL absorbs writes, manages checkpoint pressure, and handles burst-heavy workloads.

Set it too low, and aggressive flushing can throttle throughput.
Set it too high, and crash recovery can become painfully long.

Redo logs are more than crash insurance.

They are part of your write-performance architecture.

Redo logs are the shock absorbers of write-heavy MySQL. Too small, and performance jolts. Too large, and recovery drags.

Why Redo Logs Matter

InnoDB redo logs are often described as crash recovery journals, but that description undersells their real operational value.

Redo logs function as a write buffer between committed transactions and eventual data file writes.

When a transaction commits:

  • Changes are written to the redo log first
  • Dirty pages remain in memory
  • Data pages are flushed later

This write-ahead logging (WAL) design allows MySQL to:

  • Absorb bursts of write activity
  • Reduce immediate random disk writes
  • Smooth checkpoint behavior
  • Preserve durability

Redo logs act like pressure regulators in a write-heavy system.

They absorb pressure spikes so the entire system doesn’t thrash every time demand increases.

Without enough redo capacity, MySQL has less room to absorb write bursts before it must flush aggressively.

Checkpoint Age and Flushing Pressure

Redo log sizing becomes most visible when checkpoint pressure builds.

Checkpoint age represents how far current write activity has advanced beyond the last durable checkpoint:

Checkpoint Age = Current LSN - Last Checkpoint LSN

As checkpoint age approaches total redo capacity:

  • Adaptive flushing intensifies
  • Page cleaners become more aggressive
  • Dirty pages flush faster
  • Disk I/O spikes
  • Latency often becomes unstable

This is where undersized redo logs can trigger flush storms.

MySQL isn’t writing more data. It’s being forced to write sooner and less efficiently.

Useful metrics

  • Innodb_checkpoint_age
  • Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_dirty
  • Innodb_data_fsyncs
  • Innodb_log_waits

When redo space shrinks, MySQL doesn’t stop writing. It starts panicking earlier.

Symptoms of Undersized Redo

Small redo logs rarely announce themselves directly.

Instead, they often masquerade as generalized storage or write-performance issues.

Common warning signs

  • Periodic write stalls
  • Spikes in fsync activity
  • Sharp increases in page cleaner workload
  • TPS drops during burst traffic
  • Dirty page percentage volatility
  • Stable CPU, unstable write latency

A common misdiagnosis

Many systems blame disks when the real issue is insufficient redo headroom.

If writes are arriving faster than redo can comfortably buffer them, MySQL is forced into reactive flushing patterns.

The problem may not be disk speed.

It may be timing pressure.

Measuring with Status Counters

Redo log sizing should be based on observed workload, not memory percentages or inherited defaults.

Step 1: Measure redo generation rate

Use:

SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS;

Track:

  • Log sequence number
  • Log flushed up to
  • Last checkpoint at

Measure LSN growth over time:

Redo Generation Rate = (LSN delta) / elapsed time

Example

If LSN grows by 4 GB over one hour:

  • 1 GB redo capacity = frequent pressure
  • 4 GB redo capacity = ~1 hour buffer
  • 8 GB redo capacity = larger burst tolerance

Step 2: Watch for log stress

SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_log_waits';
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_os_log%';

Key metric

Innodb_log_waits

If this value increases, transactions are waiting for log free space.

That is one of the clearest signs your redo logs may be too small.

Innodb_log_waits is less a tuning suggestion and more a smoke alarm.

Practical Sizing Strategy

Forget percentage-of-RAM formulas.

Redo logs should be sized around workload intensity.

A practical starting point:

Size redo capacity to hold 30 to 60 minutes of peak redo generation

Example

Peak redo generation = 6 GB/hour

Minimum:

30 minutes = 3 GB

Safer:

60 minutes = 6 GB

Heavy burst environments:

Larger sizing may reduce flush volatility further

Trade-Offs

Smaller Redo Logs

Pros:

  • Faster crash recovery
  • Lower storage footprint

Cons:

  • Increased checkpoint pressure
  • More aggressive flushing
  • Greater write instability

Larger Redo Logs

Pros:

  • Better burst absorption
  • Smoother sustained write performance
  • Reduced flush storms

Cons:

  • Longer crash recovery
  • Delayed visibility into pressure buildup

Common Mistakes

  1. Treating redo like buffer pool sizing Redo capacity is about write throughput buffering, not memory caching.

  2. Ignoring Innodb_log_waits This can leave obvious pressure invisible until performance suffers.

  3. Oversizing without testing recovery Large redo logs may improve runtime but worsen restart scenarios.

  4. Sizing for average load instead of peak Redo logs exist to absorb pressure spikes, not calm periods.

Final Thoughts

The right redo log size isn’t about maximizing a configuration value.

It’s about matching capacity to workload behavior.

  • Too small, and MySQL becomes reactive.
  • Too large, and crash recovery becomes the hidden tax.

When redo logs are properly sized, they fade into the background.

They quietly absorb bursts, smooth checkpoint behavior, and preserve performance consistency under pressure.

Redo logs work best when they disappear into the background, quietly absorbing pressure instead of creating it.

Stop guessing.

Measure your workload, observe your log pressure, and size with intent.
